name: John Oliver
monologue: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver Season 12 Episode 2 Aired on February 23, 2025

name: John Oliver
monologue: John Oliver discusses Facebook’s controversial new plans for content moderation and which Animorphs he would and would not kill with his car.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Our main story tonight concerns technology—the thing that’s brought us stone tools, the catapults, the Tamagotchi, and one day, God willing, a fourth thing worth having.

name: John Oliver
monologue: One of the biggest stories from the last election is just how much the tech industry seemed to swing toward Trump. Elon Musk, of course, campaigned and jumped for him, and Jeff Bezos reportedly killed the Washington Post endorsement of Kamala Harris and got a prime seat at the inauguration alongside the CEOs of both Google and Apple. But one of the most visible swings came from Mark Zuckerberg. He famously banned Trump from Facebook after January 6th, but last month he was co-hosting a party at his inauguration. And just two weeks before, he made this striking announcement:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Oh, is that what you wanted to talk about? Because honestly I’d much rather discuss why you suddenly look like Eddie Redmayne was cast to play Ice Cube. You look like White Macklemore. You look like a high schooler going undercover as a different high schooler with fewer friends. But I’m sorry—you were talking about getting back to your roots.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, that is the CEO of Meta announcing that he’s getting rid of fact-checkers, and saying that he doesn’t want to be out of touch with mainstream discourse while wearing a $900,000 watch. There’s just no way any watch is worth that much, unless when you look at it, it reads: “It’s time to donate the rest of your money. You officially seem to have too much.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The changes Zuckerberg’s making are striking. A leaked training document found it’s now acceptable to say immigrants are “grubby filthy pieces of shit,” and also specifies that this slur for trans people is no longer a designated slur and is therefore allowed. As for replacing fact-checkers with Community Notes like on X, it is worth noting that hasn’t been a raging success over there, with one study finding nearly three quarters of accurate Community Notes on election misinformation never got shown to users. Remember that tweet falsely claiming Haitians were eating pets in Springfield, Ohio? That claim was rated PolitiFact’s lie of the year—but there is still no Community Note on the tweet, despite multiple attempts to add one.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And all of this is a pretty notable shift for Zuckerberg—because seven years ago, amid widespread public outcry around Facebook stoking misinformation and hatred, he went before Congress to apologize:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. It seems that Victorian ghost has made a pretty big turnaround since—both in terms of what he’s saying and how he looks. And I will admit: New Zuck does look like he’s having more fun. He’s tan. He looks like he’s shopping at stores that only take crypto, and he’s not sitting in front of Congress looking like a depressed version of the guy from the “stonks” meme.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Zuckerberg is framing all of this as merely responding to a broader cultural shift—something that he outlined naturally on Joe Rogan:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Is there anything more off-putting than a guy worth hundreds of billions trying to be a relatable everyman? You know how it is—chilling in the living room with the bros, cracking a six-pack of Ace of Spades Magnums, kicking back on your diamond-encrusted sofa, and turning on the big-screen TV, which in my house is a hollow box where I pay the cast of The Office to reenact my favorite scenes. You know—just relatable, everyday stuff, guys!

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, I’m not saying Facebook was doing a perfect job of moderating content until now—we’ve criticized them multiple times before on this show. I’m also not saying they even could have done it perfectly. It’s been said that content moderation at scale is impossible to do well. But the decision to both abandon fact-checkers and turn off systems they previously claimed made the platform safer does feel like he’s about to make that site a whole lot worse. And the self-depiction of Zuckerberg—rap name Lil’ Broccoli—as someone simply embracing his company’s “roots around free expression” is just self-serving bullshit.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So given all of that, tonight let’s take a look at the challenges of content moderation, how Facebook’s faced them in the past, and what might have led to its new approach. And let’s start with the challenges, because from the very beginning of the modern internet, there were concerns about what was on it.

name: John Oliver
monologue: In 1995, Senator James Exon brought a blue binder to the floor of the Senate. It was full of—well—

name: John Oliver
monologue: The most hardcore, perverse types of pornography.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The images came from the internet. Exon wanted his fellow Senators to realize what kids could see:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Come by my desk. Take a look at this disgusting material.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, so there’s a lot to love there—from the binder that says “WARNING” in big letters, to the invitation to “come by his desk anytime for some disgusting material,” but my favorite part has to be the clip of a Playboy JPEG loading one centimeter at a time. That is an extremely accurate portrayal of what online porn was like in the ’90s. How do I know? No reason at all.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Back then, there were battles in both Congress and the courts about how the law should treat websites’ hosting of things like pornography and defamatory comments. For a brief time, there were questions about whether a site’s decision to moderate content in any way made it a publisher, and therefore liable for anything that it didn’t remove.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That ultimately led to the passage of what’s known as Section 230 —often described as “the 26 words that created the internet.” It stated the companies could be shielded from liability for what its users post, because unlike, say, a print publisher, websites are dealing with so much material they couldn’t possibly vet all of it. It does have some carve-outs—it doesn’t give sites a pass for certain types of illegal content, like child sexual abuse and terrorism materials—but mostly, it allows them to moderate without fear.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Which is good—because as scholars will tell you, content moderation is absolutely key to making the internet bearable:

name: John Oliver
monologue: You can’t have a usable platform if you don’t do some sort of content moderation—otherwise every platform will just be porn and diet pills.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Right. That would be a problem, especially on a website like, say, LinkedIn. Although, to be honest, it might already be just porn and diet pills—I haven’t been on it in years, as I’ve had this job since 2014 and frankly have no interest in learning how other people rise and grind.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The point is though, if you want people to use your site, and crucially, have companies want to pay to advertise on it, you’re going to have to make choices about what to remove—and how you make those choices is always going to be contentious.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Facebook over the years has learned a lot of these lessons the hard way. In its early days, it took an almost touchingly naive approach, as this former employee explains:

name: John Oliver
monologue: We had to set up some ground rules—basic decency, no nudity, and no violent or hateful speech. And after that, we felt some reluctance to interpose our value system on this worldwide community that was growing.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Was there not a concern then that it could become sort of a place of just utter confusion? That you have lies that are given the same weight as truths, and that it kind of just becomes a place where truth becomes completely obfuscated?

name: John Oliver
monologue: No. We relied on what we thought were the public’s common sense and common decency to police the site.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Oh, you did, did you? I mean, I’d say that was adorable, but frankly I would be embarrassed to go on Frontline and confess that everyone working at Facebook shared a level of wide-eyed naïveté that can only be described as full-blown Amelia Bedelia.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, obviously, that initial optimism didn’t last, and over the years Facebook started implementing more and more rules and employing more and more people to enforce them. And that could be a grim job. Here is one moderator describing what it was like to screen thousands of disturbing images a day—with, I’m going to warn you, a very distracting disguise:

name: John Oliver
monologue: I think it would be easier to deal with the images if you weren’t having to think about them so deeply. I worked the evening shift, so I would start at 6:00 p.m., finish at 2:00 in the morning. But then you would often wake up three, four hours later. You’d suddenly sit up in bed remembering the decision that you’ve made and realizing that you’ve made a mistake—like, I’ve missed a nipple. You remember some image that you’ve seen, and you suddenly realized that there was a naked girl on one side or—or an ISIS flag in the background, so now it should have been deleted under the terrorism policy.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, setting aside that it’s coming from a grown man with a baby head, talking like Darth Vader while dressed for vacation—that is a depressing glimpse into what Facebook was dealing with, and it’s just a long way from relying on the inherent good of humanity to hiring people to mainline ISIS porn.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And while some decisions around blocking content were easy, others turned out to be more difficult. Because think about it: Say you ban nudity. What about statues? What about breastfeeding? What about a breastfeeding statue? And before you answer—what if I told you that I meant this one?

name: John Oliver
monologue: The company also had to develop policies around hate speech and misinformation—where the boundaries could be even trickier to define. For instance, their rules prohibited attacks on people because they belong to protected categories based on things like race, sex, gender identity, or religious affiliation. But it allowed users broader latitude when they wrote about narrower subsets of the categories.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And watching moderators try to apply rules like that in practice can be bizarre, as this hidden-camera footage from a content moderation center in Ireland shows:

name: John Oliver
monologue: That ticket there—’fuck off back to your own country,’ and it says Muslim—Oh, immigrants—

name: John Oliver
monologue: If it just said ‘Muslims,’ then yeah you’d take this action. But it doesn’t, it’s actually an ignore.

name: John Oliver
monologue: He looks after stinking Muslim immigrants. I think that’s fine.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, because saying that they’re stinking might be physical inferiority. If it said like Muslim immigrant scum, for example, that would be a delete.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, that is a weird place to draw the line. But at the same time, anywhere you draw a line can be weird. Deciding where speech becomes harmful is like trying to figure out which of the horrifying nightmares on an Animorphs cover you wouldn’t run over with your car.

name: John Oliver
monologue: These freaks? No question. It’s on sight. I’ll bounce them off the front bumper of my Subaru going 80 and feel nothing.

name: John Oliver
monologue: On the other end, though: Whoa, whoa, whoa—that’s a normal kid. Slow down. I’m not trying to do time.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But in the middle? Yeah, that’s a question, isn’t it? That’s a question.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And the thing is, the same goes with fact-checking. Obvious lies are one thing, but there are plenty of statements that are factually true but still technically misleading. And at one time, Facebook put a lot of thought into this—even producing this video in 2018, featuring a bunch of employees wrestling with the nuances of moderation, and one even diagramming out the problem as he saw it:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Imagine, on the X-axis, that you have the amount of truth in a piece of content. Now, on the Y-axis, you have the intent to mislead. You can take this chart and you can split it into four quadrants, right? On the bottom left, you have the set of things that are low-truth, but nobody was intending to mislead anything— that’s just called being wrong on the internet, and it happens. And in the bottom right, you know, it’s the set of things that have high truth—but again, nobody was trying to mislead anyone. That’s just called being right on the internet, and I’m sure it’ll happen someday. The top right—this is things that are high truth, high intent to mislead. So this is stuff like propaganda; this is stuff like cherry-picking of statistics. Now mind you, we have to be really careful here, right? Because of our commitment to free speech, everything we do here has to be incredibly, incredibly careful. But then we move to this quadrant—this is like the really dangerous quadrant, right? Low amount of truth, high intent to mislead. These are things that were explicitly designed and architected to be viral. These are the hoaxes of the world. These are things like Pizzagate. This is just false news. We have to get this right if we’re going to regain people’s trust.

name: John Oliver
monologue: You know, it is amazing that all of this started when a young man had a simple dream of ranking his classmates by fuckability—and 15 years later, a company’s struggling to stop people from accusing random pizzerias of human trafficking. A butterfly masturbates in its dorm room, and it causes a hurricane for the rest of us.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And to give that man credit, he’s genuinely wrestling with the issue there. But the company wasn’t doing that out of the goodness of its heart. Facebook had come under heavy fire for allowing fake news and hate speech to proliferate—not just in the U.S., but also abroad. We’ve talked before about how misinformation on Facebook helped fuel ethnic hatred, leading to headlines like “Facebook admits it was used to incite violence in Myanmar.

name: John Oliver
monologue: It was around this time that Zuckerberg apologized to Congress, and the company began deploying an array of options to handle misinformation—from partnering with outside fact-checkers, to appending notes to posts. It would also delete some posts or limit the reach of others. And in doing so, it found itself constantly making very hard decisions under pressure from some very powerful people. Here is one such case—and a former Facebook employee explaining the decision they ended up making:

name: John Oliver
monologue: We want to give this president the opportunity to do something historic.

name: John Oliver
monologue: This was the video of then-House Speaker Pelosi posted to Facebook in 2019—slowed down to make it seem that she was slurring her words.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Because it didn’t violate the policies that they had.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So did she put pressure on the company to take it down?

name: John Oliver
monologue: She was definitely not pleased. She definitely wanted the company—yes. And it really damaged the relationship that the company had with her.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay—set aside the fact that I don’t see why you need to slow down footage to embarrass Nancy Pelosi—a person who says plenty of embarrassing things at normal speed—I do kind of agree with Facebook there that “Does this piss off Nancy Pelosi?” isn’t a valid metric for taking that particular video down.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, I’m not saying Facebook made the right decision 100% of the time. Again, no company operating at this scale could. But it did develop systems that it claimed worked pretty well. At one point, they bragged that when people saw fact-checkers had labeled content false or partially false, they would not click on it nearly 95% of the time. In a recent report, they noted that when it comes to hate speech they take action against, their systems automatically dealt with 95.3% of it—meaning users only had to report the rest.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, of course, some of those tools are being watered down—and others are being turned off completely. And that brings us to the question of why. Why are they suddenly doing this?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Well, there are a few things that happened during the past 5 years that have helped bring us to this point. One has been conservatives repeatedly painting normal content moderation as political persecution:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Big tech’s out to get conservatives. That’s not a suspicion—that’s not a hunch—that’s a fact.

name: John Oliver
monologue: We’ve seen these, uh, these—big tech has been censoring us.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The American people are being censored. Conservatives are being censored. The information that’s flowing to the American people is being censored. It’s just the bottom line.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, that is obviously all bullshit.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But to be fair, Devin Nunes knows a thing or two about censorship—given he once filed a $250 million lawsuit against Twitter accounts that made fun of him, including one that pretended to be Nunes’s cow. He sued a fake Twitter cow because it said mean things about him, prompting the ACLU to issue this actual statement headlined:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Devin Nunes’s cow has a First Amendment right to call Representative Nunes a treasonous cowpoke.

name: John Oliver
monologue: We truly live in the single stupidest timeline.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The point is, conservatives have been crying censorship for years—but the evidence for that is very weak. First, to the extent that posts do get flagged more, that’s probably because conservatives tend to be more likely to spread political misinformation—according to numerous empirical studies. But even if you think platforms are trying to suppress conservatives, they’re doing a terrible job of that, given many of Facebook’s top performers lean right, and there are three times as many explicitly conservative news influencers as liberal ones on the site.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Nevertheless, Republicans conducted an all-out assault on the idea of content moderation, often citing one go-to example outlined here by Jeanine Pirro:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Who suppressed free speech in the 2020 election? Facebook, when they wouldn’t allow people to communicate, and the press to communicate, on Hunter Biden’s laptop.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Right—Hunter Biden’s fucking laptop. A story that Big Tech successfully censored, which is why you’ve never heard about it. And I’m afraid it is worth taking a second to remind you of the details in this story—because while people’s minds might immediately swing to “Russian hoax” or “damning evidence of Biden corruption,” the truth is it was neither.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, it eventually came out that files from the laptop were legit—but also that nothing on it revealed illegal or unethical behavior by Joe Biden.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So was initially suppressing the laptop story a fuck-up by these companies in hindsight? Yeah.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Was the story itself particularly revelatory or important? Not really.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Did Facebook’s actions prevent people from finding out about it before the election? Again—not really. Even during the period Facebook was limiting its spread, the story got 54 million views on its site. So if this was an attempt at censorship, it was successful in limiting the audience to around the same number of people that watched the fucking Friends finale.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But that initial decision meant Mark Zuckerberg got yelled at a lot by the right. And around that same time, he was also being yelled at by Biden’s White House—because as the COVID vaccine was rolling out, a lot of misinformation was circulating on Facebook. Biden himself said at one point of Facebook: “They’re killing people,” and while he quickly walked that back, to hear Zuckerberg tell it, the pressure from the White House to suppress anything critical of vaccines back then was overwhelming.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, he’s clearly pandering to Joe Rogan and his audience there—although many seem too distracted by his outfit for that to work well, given comments under that video include “Bro dressed like undercover cop,” “I thought this was Lil Dicky,” and “Why is a 40-year-old billionaire dressed like my 25-year-old shrooms guy?

name: John Oliver
monologue: But—but let’s deal with his implicit claim that the government launched investigations to punish Facebook for hosting anti-vaccine content. It is true that the government’s investigated Facebook a lot in recent years—but none of those investigations fit Zuckerberg’s narrative. Some—like an FTC antitrust lawsuit—were launched during the first Trump administration. Others—like the CFPB’s investigation of big tech payment systems—involved multiple other companies. And much of the scrutiny the company’s received in recent years was actually the result of a whistleblower releasing a cache of documents known as the Facebook Files.

name: John Oliver
monologue: As for Zuckerberg’s complaint the government was cursing and screaming at Facebook—they are allowed to do that. When we call up government agencies to check a fact, they can tell us to eat shit—because cursing does not violate your rights. For more on that, check out the Constitution for Total Fucking Dumbasses . What they can’t do is force you to do something—and in that interview, Zuckerberg describes his response to government demands back then as:

name: John Oliver
monologue: I was just like—well, we’re not going to do that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And exactly! You said no! As was your right. And don’t take my word for this: Allegations like these have been adjudicated in court. When two Republican state AGs tried suing the government, claiming it pressured platforms—including Facebook—to censor their speech, they lost in a 6–3 Supreme Court decision written by Amy Coney Barrett, who noted the plaintiffs could not demonstrate that their content was restricted due to government pressure.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look—I can understand Zuckerberg’s feelings being hurt by the president saying his company’s killing people, and—and I can understand him being sick of being yelled at by Republicans for doing too much, and by Democrats for doing too little. On some level, I can even understand a business wanting to cozy up to whoever’s in the White House.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But there is one other factor here that does seem relevant to this discussion and feels important to mention:

name: John Oliver
monologue: It’s a political evolution for Meta. Four years after Facebook suspended Mr. Trump’s account in the wake of January 6th, and just months after the president-elect accused Zuckerberg of plotting against him in 2020, calling for life in prison if Zuckerberg did it again—but after Mr. Trump’s win, Zuckerberg traveled to Mar-a-Lago, his company donated a million dollars to the Trump inaugural fund, and now close Trump ally and UFC head Dana White is joining Meta’s board.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Meta, Facebook—I think they’ve come a long way.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Do you think he’s directly responding to the threats that you have made to him in the past?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. Yeah, probably. Trump threatened Mark Zuckerberg with life in prison. Then Zuckerberg turned around, gave him money, hired one of his buddies, and changed the direction his company was going. It doesn’t take a genius to draw a conclusion there—and in fact, it didn’t take one.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And—and it didn’t stop there. Meta also recently paid $25 million to settle a bullshit lawsuit that Trump filed over being kicked off Facebook—despite many experts agreeing that was well within the company’s rights.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And at this point, it does begin to feel like Trump is doing exactly what Zuckerberg accused the Biden administration of: leveraging the power of his office to pressure social media companies to bend to his will. And Zuckerberg seems to be complying.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And he’ll insist these changes are not a result of being under political pressure—but either way, Facebook sure seems now set to become an absolute sewer of hatred and misinformation. Which, I know, sounds like a pretty good description of Facebook already—but we’re about to see what happens when they really stop trying.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So what can we do? Well, there are some bad ideas out there. Both Democrats and Republicans have, in recent years, suggested ways to amend Section 230 so companies are more liable for what appears on websites—but I am yet to see a proposal that couldn’t be easily weaponized to enable political censorship.

name: John Oliver
monologue: There are definitely options available to companies that advertise on Facebook. And I would argue they might want to seriously consider whether they want their ads next to these actual sample sentences Facebook says are now acceptable. Hey Disney, you want Olaf promoting Frozen 3 next to that shit? I don’t know, maybe you do.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But for individuals, the options here are more limited. You could delete your Meta accounts—and you would not be alone in doing that. In January, Google searches for how to cancel and delete Facebook, Instagram, and Threads accounts increased by over 5,000%. And there are alternatives out there that don’t seem as desperate to fall in line with Trump. But I do get that if Facebook and Instagram are where your family and friends are, you may not be ready to take that step. Just remember to take whatever you read on those platforms with even more of a grain of salt than you did before.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But there is one small way you can actually fuck with Meta, and that is by making yourselves a bit less valuable to them. Remember, advertising makes up 98% of Meta’s revenue, and a key component is them being able to offer companies the ability to micro-target you. Meta can do that because they track massive amounts of data about not just what you do on their sites but all across the internet—which is why they probably would not want me to tell you that you can change your settings so that Facebook and Instagram cannot profit as much from your data anymore.

name: John Oliver
monologue: If you’d be interested in the step-by-step guide on how to do that, simply visit johnoliverwantsyourraterotica.com .

name: John Oliver
monologue: And in the meantime, if Facebook is going to continue to subject us to a steadily rising tide of slurs, hoaxes, and misinformation, the least it can do is tell us the actual truth in its messaging:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Here at Facebook, it’s time to get back to our roots around free expression.

name: John Oliver
monologue: We’ve been 100% committed to making Facebook a safe and inclusive place for all people. Over the years, we’ve tried our best to prevent the site from becoming a frothing toilet of the worst humanity has to offer.

name: John Oliver
monologue: It felt like our responsibility—because we made the toilet, and got super rich from it.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But moderating billions of users is really hard. They say without it, the internet would just be porn and diet pills. God, I wish those were the only things we had to look out for. It’s porn, diet pills, hoaxes, slurs, death threats, gambling, crypto scams, those pictures of like a weirdly jacked grandpa that say “one trick to getting turbo shredded after 50″—oh, it’s a lot.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Which is why we’re so happy to announce our 2025 policy on content moderation:

name: John Oliver
monologue: To be clear, all our previous issues remain. But by strategically pivoting to “fuck it,” we’ve found it’s now more of a you problem.

name: John Oliver
monologue: It’s so nice not to have to keep all the nuances straight. Like, why “immigrants are shitty” is acceptable, but “immigrants are shit” isn’t.

name: John Oliver
monologue: You sure? I think because—oh hang on, is the adjective or the object—what if they wrote, “Go back to your country, immigrant?

name: John Oliver
monologue: You know how your older relatives would say, “I got an email from a prince in Africa who will send me a million dollars if I give him my social security number,” and you had to be like, “No grandma, that’s fake”?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Well, now you just have to do that for all your relatives—for all news, forever.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Besides, what is the worst that could happen?

name: John Oliver
monologue: We kind of sort of contributed to a genocide in Myanmar, remember?

name: John Oliver
monologue: What are the odds another genocide could happen?

name: John Oliver
monologue: I have no idea. We fired the team that would know.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’m just glad my baby’s going to grow up in a world where he can use the slurs of his choice. Or her choice. Or their—oh, right, no, that’s right. It’s two. Facebook decided it is just the two now. Hear that?

name: John Oliver
monologue: And to those who say this is just us rolling over for President Trump in the hopes he won’t throw us all in prison, let me forcefully say: Nuh-uh.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Donald Trump doesn’t set a tone here—unless he said he did. Did he?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Just know that whatever’s happening out there, we here at Facebook are recommitting to our core values—the same ones we’ve definitely always had: Freedom of expression, avoidance of responsibility, and ranking college girls by hotness.

name: John Oliver
monologue: No, no, that’s too far back. Okay, never mind.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Facebook—it’s like a town square. If your town was also full of Russian spies and bots, some teenagers disguised as adults, and some adults disguised as teenagers, getting together at all hours of the day or night to say whatever they want—including conspiracy theories, plus variations on “but the Nazis also had some good ideas.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And also now you are the mayor and police of your town square.

name: Main Segment
monologue: Online content moderation, particularly for Facebook Other segment: —

name: Zuckerberg
monologue: Hey everyone. I want to talk about something important today because it’s time to get back to our roots around free expression on Facebook and Instagram.

name: Zuckerberg
monologue: First, we’re going to get rid of fact-checkers and replace them with community notes similar to X, starting in the U.S. Second, we’re going to simplify our content policies and get rid of a bunch of restrictions on topics like immigration and gender that are just out of touch with mainstream discourse. Third, we’re changing how we enforce our policies to reduce the mistakes that account for the vast majority of censorship on our platforms. We used to have filters that scanned for any policy violation; now we’re going to focus those filters on tackling illegal and high-severity violations. And for lower severity violations, we’re going to rely on someone reporting an issue before we take action.

name: Zuckerberg
monologue: For most of our existence, we’ve focused on all the good that connecting people can do. But it’s clear now that we didn’t do enough to prevent these tools from being used for harm as well. And that goes for fake news, for foreign interference in elections, and hate speech, as well as developers and data privacy. We didn’t take a broad enough view of our responsibility. And that was a big mistake. And it was my mistake, and I’m sorry.

name: Zuckerberg
monologue: What we do is we try to build a platform that gives people a voice. But there’s this wholesale generational shift in who are the people who are being listened to. I think it’s just like a wholesale shift in saying, ‘We just want different people who we actually trust. Um, who are actually going to, like, tell us the truth. And, like, not give us, like, the opinions that you’re supposed to say, but, like, the type of stuff that I would actually—like, when I’m sitting in my living room with my friends—like, the stuff that we know is true.'

name: Zuckerberg
monologue: I mean basically these people from the Biden Administration would call up our team and like scream at them and curse. I mean Biden when he was—he gave some statement at some point, I don’t know if it was a press conference or to some journalists—where he basically was like, ‘these guys are killing people.’ And—and um—and I don’t know—then like all these different agencies and branches of government basically just like started investigating and coming after our company. It was—it was brutal. It was brutal.

name: Very Briefly
monologue: back in 2020, while Trump was president, social media sites got a warning from the FBI to look out for “hack and leak” operations before the election. Then, in October, the New York Post ran a story based on files from a laptop they claimed belonged to Hunter Biden—which had been given to them by Steve Bannon and Rudy Giuliani. Facebook and Twitter were wary of the story. Twitter briefly didn’t allow people to post links to it, and Facebook allowed the story to be seen and shared but limited the article’s reach—only to remove that restriction soon after.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver Season 12 Episode 3 Aired on March 3, 2025

name: John Oliver
monologue: John Oliver discusses tipping, why it’s more complicated and fraught than you might realize, how we can address some of the issues surrounding it, and whether or not he deserves 25% at the end of this story.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Our main story tonight concerns restaurants, one of the dumbest things we’ve used HBO’s money to pay for—tied with Russell Crowe’s jockstrap, this giant cake, and the contractual day rate of Armie Hammer (three days, plus transportation, by the way). There’s not a lot to say. More broadly, we’re going to talk about tipping.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Lately, we’re not just seeing it in restaurants—we’re being asked to do it everywhere, and people are fed up.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’m purchasing an office chair online, and they’re asking me if I want to leave a tip!” “Are we tipping at drive-throughs?” “The airport in New Jersey just asked me to tip at self-checkout—tip myself? I did all the work! Who am I tipping?” “We got Fro-Yo last night, and it was self-serve. Then, when I go to pay, the kid at the register is like, ‘It’s just going to ask you a question,’ and the question says: ‘How much tip do you want to leave?’ I was like, ‘What the fuck am I tipping you for? It was literally self-serve! I grabbed the container, I pulled the lever, I even sprinkled the cookie dough bites! If anybody’s getting a tip around here, it’s me!’

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, okay. First, nobody should ever be getting that worked up about frozen yogurt—it is ice cream for people who hate themselves. That said, I do agree that you should be able to tip yourself when you do a good job. In fact, I’m going to start something tonight: I’m putting a little bit of money into this jar every time I make a good joke or a salient point. Watch this space.

name: John Oliver
monologue: In fact, nearly three in four people think tipping culture has gotten out of control. There are so many stories of people being asked to tip in weird places—from one woman saying her mortgage company has been asking for tips lately, to another sharing how her Chevy Cruze got towed and when she went to the impound lot and it came time to pay, on the screen, additional gratuity options appeared.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And getting asked to tip at an impound lot might seem like the craziest possible example—until you see this TikTok of a fully automated coffee kiosk:

name: John Oliver
monologue: You want a fucking tip? Are you serious?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Look, I think we can all agree that is ridiculous. Especially because that piece of machinery with googly eyes doesn’t want a tip—all it wants is the sweet release of death and to be welcomed into the kingdom of heaven. But news flash, robot—that’s never going to happen. You’re not getting into heaven. You know why? Say it with me, folks:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Exactly. Bingo bango. Enjoy robot hell. Down you go. And stay there.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I will eliminate taxes on tips for restaurant workers and hospitality workers and anyone else relying on tips. No more taxes on tips. No taxes on tips. None. None!

name: John Oliver
monologue: Look, Trump may be the most predictable man who has ever lived, but at least he’s out there trying to generate suspense at random points in the middle of otherwise normal sentences.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Once every three or four minutes, he belts out a random word like he’s announcing it as the musical guest on Saturday Night Live .

name: John Oliver
monologue: But it is true—Trump has promised to eliminate taxes on tips, and Kamala Harris followed suit, adopting a similar proposal. And right now, lawmakers are deciding whether or not this proposal will make it into the budget. But the thing is, tipping is actually a lot more complicated and fraught than you may realize.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So, given that, tonight let’s talk about tipping—why we do it, what the problems with it are, and how we might be able to address at least some of them.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And let’s start with the fact that tipping here is way more pervasive than in most of the world. In Europe, tipping is much less of a norm, while in Japan, it can even be considered embarrassing and awkward. And Americans traveling abroad sometimes find wait staff confused if they try to tip, as this man discovered in Amsterdam:

name: John Oliver
monologue: We got a few beers, and I left like a five on the table. They were like, “Oh, you forgot this.” I’m like, “Oh no, that’s for you.” They said, “Why?

name: John Oliver
monologue: And you know, if they ask why , it means they’re probably getting paid fine. Like, they didn’t see that and go, “Oh yeah!

name: John Oliver
monologue: If you saw somebody in Portland and a five was on a table, and they didn’t know why, they’d be like, “All right, five bucks!

name: John Oliver
monologue: That tells you something about the culture of your economy and how you treat your workers.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Right. You know a country is in pretty good shape when their workers turn down free money.

name: John Oliver
monologue: We do not need your $5, for we are each given a fair wage, and universal healthcare, and a beautiful windmill to sleep in at night, and all the tulips that we can eat. Truly, it is paradise here in the Netherlands.

name: John Oliver
monologue: No, but while tipping is now mainly known as an American affectation, its origin is commonly traced back to Tudor England, when visitors to private homes were expected to give sums of money at the end of a visit for services rendered by the host’s servants. Hundreds of years later, visiting Americans brought the custom back home with them, and it really took off after the Civil War, when some employers hired formerly enslaved people, paid them low wages, and then encouraged customers to leave tips.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And I will say, there’s consistently been pushback against this practice.

name: John Oliver
monologue: William Howard Taft was once referred to as the “patron saint of the anti-tip crusaders”, which is a fantastic spin on ‘cheap bastard’.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Meanwhile, Ralph Waldo Emerson complained about tipping for bad service, writing:

name: John Oliver
monologue: I confess with shame that I sometimes succumb and give the dollar. Yet, it is a wicked dollar, by which, by and by, I shall have the manhood to withhold.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And while it’s fine to wish you’ll one day be strong enough to resist pressure to tip, I’m just going to say it:

name: John Oliver
monologue: That guy would have absolutely crumbled in the face of this robot. He’d have signed his house over to that googly-eyed monster, even if it got his order wrong.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The anti-tipping movement grew so pervasive in the early 20th century that six states passed laws criminalizing the practice. But that obviously did not last, and nowadays, tipping is everywhere. Though, it can seem like no one really understands the rules of when and how much to tip.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Even one of the leading academic experts on tipping has said:

name: John Oliver
monologue: I don’t know how much you’re supposed to tip, and I study this.

name: John Oliver
monologue: It’s gotten to the point where some consumers are now opting out of the system altogether, like this guy:

name: John Oliver
monologue: So, I’m not tipping anymore. I’m done. I’m out. Used to be, you would give a tip if somebody gave exceptional service. When was the last time you got exceptional service anywhere? They made food, I carried it to my table, you got me a Diet Coke—thank you, that was your job. You don’t get 25% because you did your job. And I’m not the bad guy here. I’m not!

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah… Are you 100% sure about that, though? Because you can be irritated with our current system of tipping, but protesting it by stiffing your server is about as effective as protesting police budgets by flipping off a police dog. He has nothing to do with the policy, and the only life you’re making worse is his. Also, between advocating for stiffing waiters and his ‘I Heart Fossil Fuels’ t-shirt, I’m just going to take a stab here—you might actually be the bad guy.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But, to understand why just not tipping is such a bad idea, it helps to understand exactly who works for tips and how they get paid. Because while you might primarily think of servers at restaurants, who do make up a large share of those who work for tips, tipped workers can also include:

name: John Oliver
monologue: In fact, under federal law, workers can be classified as tipped workers if they receive just $30 a month in tips. And that distinction really matters. Because in most states, employers can legally pay tipped workers a much lower base wage, as these cartoon graphics will explain:

name: John Oliver
monologue: The federal minimum wage is $7.25 per hour.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But if you’re a tipped worker, it’s $2.13 per hour—also referred to as the subminimum wage.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. The federal subminimum wage, sometimes called the tipped minimum wage, is just $2.13 an hour. And it’s been at that level since 1991. It may be the most depressing thing that we’re still having to live with from that year, were it not for the fact that 1991 was also the year that the Supreme Court was joined by this fucking guy here:

name: John Oliver
monologue: By the way, the Motorcoach option is off the table. Big mistake. Huge.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, for what it’s worth, many states choose to set a wage higher than that, but only these seven—( graphic appears )—and a handful of cities have the same minimum wage for tipped and non-tipped workers alike. Meaning that everywhere else, the expectation is that some workers can be paid less because their tips will make up the difference. But the thing is, $2.13 sometimes isn’t even enough to cover payroll taxes, as this worker explains:

name: John Oliver
monologue: In Indiana, you make $2.13 an hour.” “Two thirteen an hour?” “Yeah. You don’t see a paycheck. Your paycheck literally says, ‘This is not a check.’” “It says $0?” “This is not a check. Cuz it—it just goes to taxes. So basically, you’re starting at zero.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Right. You can literally be given a check that has “THIS IS NOT A CHECK” written on it. And come on… Who is writing those paychecks—René Magritte?!

name: John Oliver
monologue: Hi. If you’re seeing this, you have “explained the joke to me” toggled on your HBO account. René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist painter, whose most famous works include this painting of a pipe with the words “This is not a pipe” beneath it—because, of course, it isn’t a pipe. It’s a painting.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That might seem banale now, but trust me, if you were sitting in a French art museum in 1929, this blew your fucking mind. People were speaking in tongues, throwing up in response—it was a regular Rite of Spring scene.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Hi. You hit the button again. Rite of Spring is a work by Igor Stravinsky that was supposedly so avant-garde it caused riots at its first performance. Apparently, Camille Saint-Saëns stormed out of the premiere, although admittedly, that claim is now in some dispute. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I really do need to get back to the show.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Takes some fucking balls, though, right?

name: John Oliver
monologue: The point is, you can make as little as $2.13 an hour, and if what you make in tips doesn’t get you all the way up to minimum wage, theoretically , your employer is supposed to cover the difference through what is called the tip credit. But that can be hard for employers to keep track of, and it’s a system that’s easy to cheat. It’s been said that the tip credit is often abused at the employees’ expense, with one restaurant worker saying:

name: John Oliver
monologue: As long as I’ve been doing this, I have never, ever—not one time—met anyone who’s been compensated for a below-minimum pay period.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So the fact is, a lot of tipped workers’ pay may come down to how much someone chooses to leave as gratuity.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And if you’ve ever worked for tips, you know you can do very well—though that can depend on not just where you work, but when you work, or even what mood your customers happen to be in.

name: John Oliver
monologue: As this former hospitality worker explains:

name: John Oliver
monologue: If you come in on a Tuesday—I mean, some people party on a Tuesday, but not as much as Saturday. Put yourself in a tipped worker’s shoes: could you survive off of $2.50 an hour and rely on the drunk guy in front of you to pay your rent?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Right. Someone’s ability to pay their rent can be dependent on a person who may be drunk or partying on a Tuesday—or, if they happen to be the current Defense Secretary, very likely both.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And all this might help explain why recent analyses have found that poverty rates for tipped workers are over twice as high as for non-tipped workers. And some tend to be more disadvantaged by this than others. Studies have found that both Black and white consumers tip white servers more than Black ones. And one paper found that waitresses in their 30s, and those with large breasts, blonde hair, and/or slender bodies, received larger average tips than their counterparts without these characteristics. And look, it is not news that life is somewhat easier for attractive people. I would know—I was featured in Vogue in 2015 in a gallery titled, and this is true:

name: John Oliver
monologue: 10 Unconventional Alternatives to the Sexiest Man Alive.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Who was, at the time, by the way, David Beckham.

name: John Oliver
monologue: You know, life is just different for us—whether you’re the sexiest man alive or his, quote, “unconventional alternative.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But obviously, those higher tips can come with a lot of unwanted harassment. And if servers are making a subminimum wage, they might feel especially pressured to put up with that in order to make a living. And there is one final twist here, which is that a server’s tips may not even be entirely theirs. In some restaurants, there’s an expectation that servers will “tip out”—or share a portion of their tips with other restaurant personnel. And depending on how that’s set up, it can really put servers in a bind. Here’s that woman you saw a minute ago, explaining how it worked for her:

name: John Oliver
monologue: You have to tip out. I mean, most restaurants, it’s roughly 3 to 5% of your sales. So, like—even if people are tipping the 20% that is standard for great service, most servers are tipping out 3 to 5% of that to busers, hosts, and bartenders.

name: John Oliver
monologue: What if I leave you nothing? What happens?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Then we still have to pay that tip out—whether you give us money or not. So, say your bill is $100, and I have to tip out 5%. If you don’t tip me at all, I’m paying $5 to wait on you out of my own pocket.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That is true at some places. Not only are you subsidizing the servers, but they may be subsidizing other members of staff, too. And if that seems less like a business and more like an insane money carousel, where everyone is paying everyone else and somehow everyone is still poor— Welcome to the restaurant industry.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And at this point, you might be thinking:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Well, fuck this whole system . Why don’t we just get rid of it?

name: John Oliver
monologue: And you would not be the first to suggest that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Here’s that guy you saw earlier, gaming out the system he’d rather see:

name: John Oliver
monologue: If you own a restaurant, just tell me what it costs. I don’t want people to go hungry. What does it cost for me to get my food—and also so that the waitstaff doesn’t have to join the cartel, do some Lord of the Flies, Oliver Twist-like—I want people to be taken care of. Just tell me what it costs!

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, that might sound reasonable—

name: John Oliver
monologue: ( The paying a fair price for what I’m getting part, not the absolute avalanche of fearing that waitstaff would “join the cartel” or do some Lord of the Flies or Oliver Twist-like thing—whatever the f uck that could mean.)

name: John Oliver
monologue: I don’t know what versions of either of those books he’s read, but Lord of the Flies and Oliver Twist had some very different answers for what children will get up to when unsupervised—and neither of them seem like they’d apply to workers making the tipped minimum wage.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But unfortunately, when many people say “Just tell me what it costs”, they also mean:

name: John Oliver
monologue: And it better cost exactly the same, or I am going to be pissed.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’ve done the research where I give people hypothetical menus:

name: John Oliver
monologue: He then asked people how expensive they thought the restaurant was. People overwhelmingly thought the menu with the 15% higher prices was more expensive than a menu where they would tip 15% or more anyway.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, even if the amount of money coming out of your pocket is the exact same both times, people view the menu with built-in tip prices as more expensive—because it just feels more expensive. It’s sort of the same way that it feels like I’m older than David Beckham—even though, fun fact, I’m two years younger than him. He’s aging incredibly, and I think I’m… tickling ?

name: John Oliver
monologue: And that has led people to try and come up with other ways to relieve the financial stress on tipped workers, which brings us all the way back to Trump’s promise to eliminate taxes on tips. It’s an idea that he was proud to reveal had a notable celebrity backer:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [TRUMP] “On your receipt, when you get your receipt for a restaurant—you know who sent me one? Kid Rock! How good is Kid Rock, isn’t he? But he sent me a receipt, and he wrote on the receipt: ‘Vote for Trump and you won’t pay taxes on tips.’ He wrote that on the receipt. I said, ‘That’s very smart. That’s very smart. Smart guy.’

name: John Oliver
monologue: So for restaurant workers, for hotel workers, for caddies—for car people—it’s a lot! But anybody receiving tips—there’s no more tax on tips! And I think that’s going to be a great thing!

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, there is so much to deal with there— From the phrase “car people,” to (again) the surprise punctuation on “caddies,” to the fact that the President is taking policy advice from Kid Rock—

name: John Oliver
monologue: A man who constantly looks like he’s on trial for something called moonshine fraud.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But the thing is, that idea has broad support. It’s a proposal supported by roughly three in four Republicans, Democrats, and Independents.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, I’m all for giving a tax break to low-wage workers, but you should know:

name: John Oliver
monologue: A lot of economists have major concerns with this particular policy—starting with the fact that the tax relief it gives would be haphazard at best.

name: John Oliver
monologue: One of the ways to make taxes fair is to make sure that people of the same income level are paying approximately the same amount of taxes.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And in this case, you really wouldn’t be doing that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But I can’t think of a good reason why you’d want to give a tax break to the person who delivers food, but not to the person who delivers mail.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Right. That doesn’t make much sense, does it? If someone delivering packages for Amazon makes the same as someone delivering food for DoorDash, it doesn’t feel fair for one of them to be taxed significantly more.

name: John Oliver
monologue: ( Although, if we’re going to be even fairer, we’d probably tax the guy who owns the company that sends out those packages a ton more as well. But that’s not what we’re talking about tonight. )

name: John Oliver
monologue: The point is, Trump’s plan would essentially be a tax break for only the 2.5% of American workers who work for tips. And not even all of those—given that more than a third of tipped workers had incomes low enough that they face no federal income tax to begin with.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And that’s not the only issue with this idea. It’s also a policy that could be exploited. For instance:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Prompts to tip could start showing up in whole new categories of consumer transactions.

name: John Oliver
monologue: ( So you might actually be prompted to tip even more than you are right now. )

name: John Oliver
monologue: The point is, while “No tax on tips” is an easy applause line at rallies, it wouldn’t be nearly as effective as it sounds. If you really want to give relief to tipped workers, I’d argue the solution would be to eliminate the subminimum wage.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Everyone gets at least the minimum wage, and then your tip goes on top of that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: It’s a proposal that this advocacy group [OFW – One Fair Wage] has been pushing for nationwide. But I will acknowledge—not everyone is on board with this idea.

name: John Oliver
monologue: In Michigan, there’s been an ongoing fight over raising its subminimum wage, and even some who might stand to benefit do have concerns:

name: John Oliver
monologue: That’s what keeps my lights on. That’s what keeps me going back, for sure.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Because she makes tips, her minimum wage is about $4 an hour.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Soon, that’ll change, and she’ll make minimum wage like any other worker—which, right now, is roughly $10 an hour in Michigan.

name: John Oliver
monologue: When people start to realize you’re making hourly wages, um… they’ll tip less. They’ll be like, ‘Wow, they’re already making their minimum wage, which is 10-something an hour.’

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, I could see worrying about that. And while I’m not saying it’s the only reason she feels that way, having what seems to be her boss standing 3 feet away, staring daggers at the camera, might also have something to do with it. But I do get those concerns. Although it is worth remembering:

name: John Oliver
monologue: There are seven states that haven’t had a subminimum wage for decades. And yet… people still tip there.

name: John Oliver
monologue: In fact, one study found that tipped workers in those states typically earn 10 to 20% more in wages and tips.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And I’m not saying switching over is easy. There are good-faith concerns from restaurant owners, who are often operating on very thin margins, about what sudden pay hikes could mean. That’s why, in many places where the subminimum wage has been eliminated, it’s been done gradually—so that restaurants can figure out an approach that works for them, like:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Where it’s been done, the restaurant industry hasn’t imploded.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Flagstaff, Arizona, has been incrementally doing away with its subminimum wage since 2017—and both:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Meanwhile, Washington, D.C. is now two years into its phase-out, so it’s still too early to know the full impact. But numbers currently don’t show any obvious problems on the jobs front:

name: John Oliver
monologue: But maybe the clearest expression of the difference eliminating the subminimum wage can make is looking at states that have done it vs. their neighboring states that haven’t.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Just watch as a waitress in Wisconsin—which still has a subminimum wage for tipped workers—is asked about Minnesota, which got rid of it:

name: John Oliver
monologue: That’s not great. You shouldn’t lose thousands of dollars just because you’re in Wisconsin—especially because those dollars are actually more useful there. Because Wisconsin is where the National Mustard Museum is.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That’s the kind of thing you want some extra cash for!

name: John Oliver
monologue: So, when you take all of this together, a few things are clear about tipping:

name: John Oliver
monologue: 1. It’s unlikely to ever go away completely. At this point, it’s just too culturally ingrained, no matter what happens.

name: John Oliver
monologue: 2. It isn’t really a “gratuity” anymore. In a lot of places, it’s an absolute necessity. So, if you’re eating at a restaurant, you have to tip.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And there are other jobs where that might also be the case—up to and including:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now… does that mean you should also be tipping at an impound lot? NO! Absolutely not. Should you be tipping this robot? Fuck NO! That shouldn’t happen under any circumstances. That robot should go to hell. And it will.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But if you didn’t know that workers in most states rely on tips to make up for subminimum wages, well… Now you do. And if you’d rather a tip be just a little bonus, instead of critical to someone’s survival— That’s great! That means you support eliminating the subminimum wage—and you should feel free to yell at your state and federal lawmakers about it. But if you’re considering withholding tips to prove some kind of point about the unfairness of the industry… I hate to say it— You might be the bad guy.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Anyway, that is the end of this story. And it’s the end of this episode. For those of you at home, your screen’s just going to ask you a question real quick— Just go ahead and tap to make your selection. No pressure. But we worked pretty hard. And if you fell asleep, but there is a cat that’s still awake in your home… Just mash your little paws at the screen. D-D—Daddy wants some money. That’s our show! Thanks so much for watching. We’ll see you next week. Good night!

name: John Oliver
monologue: ( Not 15% over here—we’ll take the 25%, please! We worked hard this week! Get it, get it, get it, get it! Cat—25—25—get it! Get it! )

monologue: Tipping Other segments: The Silicon Valley Auto Show, 2025 Trump–Zelenskyy meeting, Kash Patel and Dan Bongino’s leadership at the FBI

name: The Point Is
monologue: people are furious at how often they’re seeing the tip screen. It is now the least welcome way to encounter an iPad in public, outside of that guy watching Pornhub on the bus .

name: The Point Is
monologue: you’re not wrong for thinking tip requests are showing up in more places. But as frustrating as that can be, lots of people depend on tips for their livelihood. And this subject took center stage last year when Trump made this bold promise:

name: Interviewer
monologue: What if someone said to you, ‘Wow, we’re going to be just like your neighbors over there in Minnesota, and you’re going to get minimum wage as your base salary plus your tips’?

name: Waitress
monologue: I would love that! I actually know some people who, um, used to work in Minnesota as servers. And then they came over here… and they realized that they’re only making $2.33. And they’re like, ‘I’m literally losing thousands of dollars by coming over here in Wisconsin.’

name: John Oliver
monologue: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver Season 12 Episode 4 Aired on March 9, 2025

name: John Oliver
monologue: John Oliver discusses ICE detention facilities, who’s in them, who runs them and – of course – why it is totally understandable if our studio audience would rather watch Drew Barrymore’s show instead.

name: John Oliver
monologue: [John] Our main story tonight concerns immigration—the surprising subject of the White House’s actual Valentine’s Day tweet, which read:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Roses are red, violets are blue, come here illegally and we’ll deport you.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Though, I guess that’s exactly the kind of romance you’d expect from a house occupied by this loving couple.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Since Trump took office, he’s made a big show of having ICE conduct immigration raids, often with news cameras and even Dr. Phil tagging along to try and generate positive coverage—though it hasn’t always gone well. For instance, they raided apartment complexes in Colorado that were supposedly centers of gang activity, only to return with very few arrests and some humiliating footage.

name: John Oliver
monologue: As the team went door to door, they found blood-stained walls but no gang members. The entire complex was virtually empty. At a second Trende Raglink complex, ICE was met by activists who taunted them:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Applause] “What the f* is wrong with you? Get out of our community!”**

name: John Oliver
monologue: Excellent! We all need more of that woman’s energy. I don’t know what she has in that mug, but I do know what she doesn’t have—any f*s left to give.**

name: John Oliver
monologue: These raids are in fulfillment of Trump’s campaign promise to implement the largest deportation operation in American history. And to do that, it seems every week he devises a new place to send migrants—from Costa Rica, to Panama, to even this:

name: John Oliver
monologue: The latest piece of the mass deportation puzzle: bringing as many as 30,000 criminal migrants to the Navy base at Guantanamo Bay.

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Trump] “So we’re going to send them out to Guantanamo. This will double our capacity immediately, right? And tough—that’s a tough—that’s a tough place to get out of.

name: John Oliver
monologue: [John] I mean… yeah, it is. Although calling GMO (Guantanamo Bay) a tough place to get out of is a bit of an understatement.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Last month, Trump actually flew 178 Venezuelan migrants there—only to quickly reverse course and fly them out after the administration started facing lawsuits. And look, most experts agree that for both legal and logistical reasons, GMO is unlikely to house 30,000 migrants anytime soon.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And what that means is most of the people who get arrested are going to be funneled into our existing immigration detention facilities.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I know we’ve talked on this show a lot about our immigration system’s problems before:

name: John Oliver
monologue: But tonight, we’re going to focus very narrowly on detention centers. They don’t tend to get talked about much, despite the fact that a lot of people go through them.

name: John Oliver
monologue: ICE currently has the budget to hold just over 41,000 people on any given day, and last year, more than 260,000 people cycled through ICE detention in total.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But Trump is already talking about sending even more people into that system, which in some quarters is cause for celebration.

name: John Oliver
monologue: After the election, stock prices for private prison companies like GEO Group and CoreCivic soared—with their CEOs each bragging to investors about how much money they were going to make:

name: John Oliver
monologue: The GEO Group was built for this unique moment in our company’s and country’s history, and the opportunities that it will bring.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’ve worked at CoreCivic for 32 years, and this is truly one of the most exciting periods in my career with the company.

name: John Oliver
monologue: [John] Look, as a general rule, if something happens that causes a private prison company to get really excited, that thing was bad.

name: John Oliver
monologue: If you ever come home and your spouse tells you:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Honey, I did something today, and the GEO Group is super excited about it.

name: John Oliver
monologue: You are in for a relationship-altering conversation.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And the thing is, immigration detention facilities are by law not supposed to be a punishment. ICE’s own website even states that detention is non-punitive.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Though, as you’re about to see, that’s like claiming that:

name: John Oliver
monologue: It is a bold assertion, sharply undercut by empirical evidence.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So, given all of that, tonight, let’s talk about ICE detention facilities and try to answer a few basic questions:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Trump and those around him often try and sell their immigration roundups as being about cracking down on crime.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Here’s his press secretary answering a question about exactly who was arrested in the first round of ICE raids:

name: John Oliver
monologue: The 3,500 arrests ICE has made so far since President Trump came back into office.

name: John Oliver
monologue: [John] Well, hold on, because that is not actually true.

name: John Oliver
monologue: While entering the U.S. without authorization can be a criminal offense, many of those who are undocumented entered legally and overstayed their visas. Simply being undocumented is a civil violation, not a criminal one.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That is an important distinction that her boss should frankly understand—given that he has committed both.

name: John Oliver
monologue: As of last year, almost half of those in ICE custody were seeking asylum. And that is actually true for some of those who got scooped up in Colorado last month.

name: John Oliver
monologue: One man got detained even though he had done everything he was supposed to do. He committed no crimes and had an asylum hearing court date. And yet, despite that, listen to his brother describe what happened:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Testimony] On Wednesday, Luis’s brother, Yonathan, was driving him to work.

name: John Oliver
monologue: No ID, though. ID—they didn’t even get past the parking lot at the Cedar Run apartment complex, where ICE detained at least five people as part of a raid Wednesday.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Luis says ICE officers wouldn’t accept his brother’s paperwork even though he showed his asylum documents as he waited on a work permit.

name: John Oliver
monologue: He has so many questions about how his brother was detained without a criminal record.

name: John Oliver
monologue: If he doesn’t have a deportation order, how can they take him?

name: John Oliver
monologue: [John] Yeah, that’s a good question. It’s actually one of many things I find hard to understand about watching that—including why those agents were wearing camouflage while doing it.

name: John Oliver
monologue: You’re in a parking lot, not dense foliage. If you actually wanted to blend in, you should have dressed up like a Claire’s accessories store in a strip mall.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The thing is, holding someone in detention is only meant to be done in limited circumstances, like if they’re a flight risk or to make sure they show up for an immigration hearing.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But the vast majority do show up for those hearings because they want their case heard.

name: John Oliver
monologue: For those with asylum claims—like that guy’s brother—a recent study found that of those who weren’t detained, 95% attended all of their Immigration Court hearings.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, there are some immigrants who are subject to what’s called mandatory detention, like if they’ve been accused of breaking the law.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That used to be confined to serious offenses like murder or gun trafficking, but that all changed when Bill Clinton expanded it to also cover minor crimes—from low-level drug convictions to writing a bad check.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And those convictions don’t even have to be recent.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Take this man, who was brought from Jamaica to the U.S. by his family when he was a teenager. He served in the military, but after completing his service, pled guilty to marijuana possession in 1997.

name: John Oliver
monologue: He moved on, started a business and a family—but then, in 2010, this suddenly happened:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Testimony] “About 5:30 in the morning, I heard a big knock on the door—BOOM BOOM BOOM BOOM.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And I opened the door, and then it was like—‘Did you apply for citizenship like six months ago?’

name: John Oliver
monologue: And they were like—‘Turn around. That’s why we’re here.’

name: John Oliver
monologue: I didn’t think that in 2010, the marijuana conviction that happened 14 years ago would have come back to haunt me.

name: John Oliver
monologue: No one should be punished for a minor mistake they made 14 years earlier—otherwise, I’d have hell to pay for playing Vanity Smurf in the 2011 Smurfs movie.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I was already punished when I saw it—and again when I had to pose for this press photo.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The point is, that Clinton-era expansion supercharged the detained population, which passed 20,000 in 2001, only to expand through Bush, Obama, Trump, and Biden to the point where we now have the world’s largest immigration detention system.

name: John Oliver
