name: John Oliver
monologue: But he does have a lot to be happy about. In order for Skydance to get its merger approved by Brendan Carr’s FCC, it committed to adopt measures that can root out the “bias that has undermined trust in the national news media.” One of those measures was installing this former conservative think-tank CEO as CBS News’s new ombudsman.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But this Monday, Ellison took a much bigger step.

name: John Oliver
monologue: A major shift in the landscape of TV news — Paramount Skydance announcing that they’ve made Bari Weiss editor-in-chief of CBS News and acquired her online news and commentary organization, The Free Press. She’s a registered independent who at one point called herself politically homeless, unrepresented by the two main U.S. parties.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, first — “politically homeless” sounds like how you’d describe Rudy Giuliani’s current fashion sense.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Paramount has bought The Free Press for $150 million, and Bari Weiss, its co-founder, will now be setting the editorial strategy, vision, and focus for CBS Mornings , CBS Evening News , Face the Nation , and even 60 Minutes.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Also, instead of reporting to the president of CBS News, Weiss will apparently report directly to David Ellison.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, if you’re not familiar with Bari Weiss, you should know she’s a proud contrarian who, in public appearances, will inevitably deliver some version of this pitch:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] I confound people because I’m Jewish. I’ve always thought I was liberal. I’m gay. I’m married to a woman. Like, that’s my life. You would think that I’m liberal and I would just go along with the flow. It’s like, I look like them, I think like them, I eat at the same restaurants. But I don’t think all the same things, and I’m not scared to say when I disagree. And I think that’s really pissed people off throughout my career.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, first — and least importantly — the reboot of Between Two Ferns looks terrible.

name: John Oliver
monologue: she’s a liberal who’s brave enough to disagree with other liberals. And along the way, she’s accumulated admirers from Jeff Bezos to Meghan McCain, and from Amy Coney Barrett to Joe Rogan.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And if you’re thinking, “Wow, that’s not a very ideologically broad ‘from’ and ‘to,’” you’re starting to catch on — because there are times where she’s a little more explicit about what she believes, like when she gave a speech to the Conservative Federalist Society featuring this fun joke:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] I am a gay woman who is moderately pro-choice. I know that there are some people in this room who don’t believe that my marriage should have been legal, and that’s okay, because we’re all Americans who want lower taxes.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Good one! And you can almost hear that room unclench after she basically says, “I know you think I deserve fewer rights, but don’t worry, besties — we’ll still chill.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And while that is obviously framed as a joke, it’s also a setup to her saying, “In all seriousness, I am here because I know that in the fight for the West, who my allies really are.

name: John Oliver
monologue: She goes on to say, “Among other things, the wave of so-called progressive prosecutors has proven to be an immensely bad thing for law and order.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And I’ve got to say, for someone who claims they’re politically homeless, she sure seems awfully at home in that room.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, this isn’t the first time an outsider billionaire has tried thumbing the scale of a news organization. We’ve seen Jeff Bezos increasingly meddle with The Washington Post , and Patrick Soon-Shiong do the same at The L.A. Times. But this feels like the most sweeping change yet — and at one of the few remaining prestige names in news.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And if one person has suddenly been handed this much power over an entire news organization, it’s worth knowing who that one person is.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So tonight, let’s take a look at Bari Weiss.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Let’s start with the fact that she’s been given editorial control of a massive news organization even though she’s never run a TV network, has no experience directing television coverage, and — as one 60 Minutes producer pointed out — is not even a reporter.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That’s true. She didn’t come up through the news side of a newspaper, but through the opinion pages — which are a very different thing. She really made a name for herself after being hired by the New York Times op-ed page in 2017. And to hear her tell it, it was for a pretty simple reason:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] To put it bluntly, I was brought in along with Bret Stephens from the Wall Street Journal as a kind of intellectual diversity hire. My job explicitly was to bring in voices that wouldn’t otherwise naturally appear in the New York Times — either because other editors wouldn’t think to commission them, or the writers themselves would think, “ The New York Times would never accept me.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. She was apparently tasked with finding voices that the Times op-ed page would never accept — which is already a big claim, given that before she got hired there, it had published op-eds from, and this is true, Muammar Gaddafi and Vladimir Putin.

name: John Oliver
monologue: If the Times had been around in the 15th century, I’m guessing it would’ve given an opinion piece to Vlad the Impaler: “Drinking the blood of my enemies isn’t disgusting — it’s beautiful and courageous.

name: John Oliver
monologue: In any case, Weiss started getting attention at the Times for writing provocative pieces — like this one, in which she argued that the left had gone too far in policing cultural appropriation.

name: John Oliver
monologue: This one — a largely sympathetic profile of the Intellectual Dark Web, a term that she popularized for people like Jordan Peterson and Ben Shapiro.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And this one — suggesting progressives were so focused on labeling fellow Americans fascists that they missed opportunities to call out real fascism, which is just some weapons-grade whataboutism.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That piece, by the way, also got attention for the fact that Weiss linked to posts from the “official Antifa Twitter account,” which was actually a well-known hoax site.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Which is pretty embarrassing. You don’t expect a Times writer to fall for online hoaxes like she’s your 75-year-old aunt on Facebook who keeps posting that message saying, “I hereby state that I do not give my permission to use any of my personal data or photos.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That is fake, Linda. Also, why would anybody steal your photos? You exclusively post pictures of your elderly cat. You’re going to be fine.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But things came to a head in 2020, after the Times ran this infamous Tom Cotton op-ed in which he argued that the U.S. should send federal troops into cities to tamp down protests against police violence.

name: John Oliver
monologue: A lot of staffers at the Times argued that it shouldn’t have published that editorial — and Bari Weiss wrote a series of tweets about a supposedly heated staff meeting, characterizing it as a civil war between “the mostly young wokes” and “the mostly 40-and-up liberals.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That claim was strongly disputed by others at the paper, with one editor saying, “I’m in the same meeting that Bari appears to be live-tweeting. This is inaccurate in both characterizations. It’s not a civil war — it’s an editorial conversation, and it’s not breaking down along generational lines.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So, to be fair, it seems Bari Weiss does have some reporting experience — specifically, trying to report what was happening in a meeting, only to have her own coworker say, “Hey, what the fuck are you talking about?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Shortly after that, she resigned, posting a lengthy resignation letter to her website, claiming that her foray into “wrongthink” had made her the subject of “constant bullying by colleagues who disagreed with my views.

name: John Oliver
monologue: She now tells the story of that letter in some pretty self-mythologizing terms:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] I thought to myself, I have a choice to make. I can stay — and in where I lived on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, Seinfeld territory — telling people you worked at The New York Times really meant something. It got you a good table at a good restaurant, among other things. And it meant a lot to me because I felt like, wow, I made it. Or I could leave, and give up the prestige, give up the platform, have no plan for what I’m doing next — but leave with my integrity. So I left with a resignation letter sort of heard around the world. It was my Jerry Maguire moment.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, self-aggrandizing bullshit aside, let’s not reduce the Upper West Side to just Seinfeld territory. It’s the site of many other cultural touchstones — like You’ve Got Mail , Will and Grace , and that time, the night before the Macy’s Parade, when balloon Spider-Man made an absolute meal out of Uncle Sam’s ass.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Anyway, she quickly launched her own publication — first as a Substack called Common Sense , and later as a full-blown media company, The Free Press. Its first motto was “Honest news for sane people,” which feels scientifically engineered to trigger an eye roll.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Here she is, not long after starting it, making her pitch:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] I want to create the media company where people can go for the best podcasts, the best reporting, the best analysis — basically combining the blue-chip, high-quality of the old media landscape with the punk energy of the new political realignment.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, first — it is pretty hard to claim you’ve got “punk energy” when you essentially spout conservative talking points while dressed like the front desk manager at a Courtyard Marriott.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I, for one, do not trust the punk bona fides of anyone wearing an Ann Taylor Collus silk blouse.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But it turns out, like most punk rock things, The Free Press was quickly bankrolled by a string of reactionary billionaires, like venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and David Sacks.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And in the five years since, it’s grown to roughly 1.5 million readers — although only around one in ten actually pay to subscribe — meaning it generates subscription revenues of about $15 million a year. Which isn’t nothing, but I would argue it’s also not quite enough to justify someone spending $150 million to acquire it, as that is a revenue-to-valuation ratio that would make Mr. Wonderful start vomiting blood.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Anyway, Weiss has since stocked The Free Press with staffers who, in some cases, are quick to brag that — like her — they are proud refugees from the mainstream media:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Hey, I’m Lucy. I’m the social media editor here at The Free Press. And today I’m going to ask my co-workers the moment they realized they were free pressers. Olivia, when did you realize that you were a free presser? Um, when I was reporting for — [bleep] — on President Trump, and they inserted the word “racist” into the headline.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, so just to be clear, she was apparently reporting for NPR, even though that bleep makes it seem like she used to write for an outlet called The Fuck-Hole Times or something.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And the word “racist” was atop a story of hers about public response to Trump saying that these four members of Congress — all American citizens, three of whom were born in the U.S. — should “go back to the countries they came from.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And I guess, if you’re not ready to call that racist, The Free Press might be the place for you.

name: John Oliver
monologue: One of Bari Weiss’s go-to lines is that she’s only interested in “the truth.” In announcing her decision to go to CBS this week, she said, “America cannot thrive without common facts, common truths, and a common reality.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Which sounds great — but watch her articulate The Free Press’s approach to arriving at the truth, and see if you can spot a small problem with it:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] The identity of our brand is truth-seeking, and our premise is you cannot get to truth in an echo chamber. The only way that you get to truth is by sitting next to someone—this is what makes it so different from any newsroom I’ve ever worked in—

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] —sitting next to someone who disagrees with you…

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] …and collaborate with them.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. I mean, maybe that is how you do it as an opinion writer, but that is not how you get to truth as a reporter, is it? You do that by leaving the newsroom and reporting. That’s not saying, “The only way to hold Henry Kissinger’s skull in your hand is by sitting next to someone who disagrees with you.” No — that’s not it. You do that by leaving your desk, breaking into Dick Cheney’s house, going into his master bathroom, and taking it out of its jar.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And I’ll be honest — there’s not a ton of hard journalism on The Free Press site. There’s really not much of anything there. There’s usually just a handful of new posts a day, which can even include weird editorial cartoons from David Mamet, the playwright. And if you’re thinking, “I didn’t realize David Mamet could draw,” fun fact: he can’t.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But don’t worry, because that hasn’t stopped him from producing cartoons like this one that says, “What’s the best way to deal with detractors?” — with the answer being “A manual for tractors.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Or this one, supposedly about environmentalism, that just says, “Shoving eggs up the tushies of chickens.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Or this one, An Autobiography by Kermit the Frog , with a blurb that says “Ribbiting” — which I’m worried might actually be too funny.

name: John Oliver
monologue: There are also a ton of first-person clickbait essays, with titles like:

name: John Oliver
monologue: I Can Explain Why the Nazi Salute Is Back.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I Took Religion Out of Christmas. I Regret It.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I Want People to Have More Kids. Does That Make Me Far-Right?

name: John Oliver
monologue: I Was Called an Inbred Swine at Princeton Last Night.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’m 17 and I’m Immunized from Woke Politics.

name: John Oliver
monologue: My Family Was Hunted by Nazis, But I Was Fired for Defending Hitler.

name: John Oliver
monologue: My Husband Wants to Be Cremated. I’d Ignore His Dying Wish.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I Used to Hate Trump. Now I’m a MAGA Lefty.

name: John Oliver
monologue: At this point, it feels like we’re just two weeks away from them posting an article titled, “I Dressed My Dead Wife Up as Hitler for Her Funeral, and Now Her Woke Family Is Mad at Me.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, if you go to the homepage of The Free Press , it might not immediately read as a particularly conservative outlet. But once you start reading its articles, the pronounced theme that starts to emerge is “the left has gone too far.” Basically, whatever issue you feel like that’s true for — Israel, campus politics, DEI, or police reform — you’ll find articles there to reinforce that opinion.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, I’m not saying the left never goes too far, or that it’s immune from criticism at all. But it can sometimes feel like The Free Press’s conclusions get out ahead of its evidence.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Which brings us to the fact that some of its pieces can be pretty poorly fact-checked — and in ways that feel important.

name: John Oliver
monologue: First, take one of its biggest splashes: this article — “I Thought I Was Saving Trans Kids, Now I’m Blowing the Whistle.

name: John Oliver
monologue: It’s an account by Jamie Reed, who’d worked as a caseworker at the Washington University Transgender Center. Her piece claimed that the clinic was harming patients by, among other things, routinely approving adolescents for medical transitions without proper mental health assessments, calling its work “morally and medically appalling.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, that story understandably got a ton of attention — including from public officials — which prompted Weiss to go on Megyn Kelly’s podcast to take something of a victory lap:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] The day after the piece published, I’ve never seen such a sort of rapid reaction to a piece of journalism. Missouri’s Attorney General announced an investigation into the gender clinic. The reason that this story was especially important and gratifying for us to have substantiated was because it’s exactly the kind of story that we exist to pursue. It’s exactly the kind of morally knotty story that journalists avoid pursuing because they know they’ll be punished or smeared for doing so. That is why The Free Press exists.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Wow, that is an exceptional amount of self-congratulation — and the bar was already set at the Jerry Maguire moment heard around the world.

name: John Oliver
monologue: the state Attorney General apparently found that article, to borrow a term, ribbiting , because they soon announced an investigation into the center.

name: John Oliver
monologue: It ultimately stopped treating minors, with Reed’s claims even being used to help justify a statewide ban on gender-affirming care for them.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So, it did have real impact — which is what makes it so awkward that when Washington University conducted its own investigation, they found that allegations of substandard care causing adverse outcomes for patients at the center were unsubstantiated.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And when other outlets reported the story out again and again, their findings did not match what The Free Press published.

name: John Oliver
monologue: For instance, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch found dozens of former patients and parents at the clinic who told them their experiences sharply contradicted the examples supplied by Reed.

name: John Oliver
monologue: NBC spent two months reaching out to nearly 40 people associated with the center and got the same result — with patients and parents saying the care they received was thorough and slow.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And the Missouri Independent found parents who told them any treatments their kids received were only undertaken after long consultations with doctors and mental health professionals — and often, patients were told they needed to wait four years.

name: John Oliver
monologue: In fact, at worst, follow-up reporting showed that as more patients sought care, the clinic became overwhelmed as its employees grappled with how best to help patients.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And to be fair, the Times did find some former patients who had complaints, including one who’d since detransitioned and felt there’d been a major lack of care and consideration from the center.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But even that article — which Weiss claimed vindicated their story — said it’s clear the clinic benefited many adolescents, with patients and parents saying their experiences were overwhelmingly positive.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And the thing is, some of Reed’s marquee examples just don’t hold up on further inspection.

name: John Oliver
monologue: For instance, she cited the harrowing story of a patient she claimed suffered liver toxicity from medication she was prescribed at the center, and whose mother was so distraught she sent a message saying they were lucky her family was not the type to sue.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That sounds pretty striking. But when the Times spoke with that family, they were stunned to read this characterization of their daughter’s case — saying she only experienced liver problems after getting COVID and taking another drug with possible liver side effects.

name: John Oliver
monologue: As for threatening a lawsuit, they were adamant that never happened — to the point they went on local news to refute the whole story:

name: John Oliver
monologue: You can’t see their faces — we’re in shadow, but we’re not hiding. But you can hear their voices.

name: John Oliver
monologue: There’s lies, and people have paid for that in the transgender community.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Did you ever say that you were going to sue the clinic, or ever allude to suing the clinic?

name: John Oliver
monologue: The parents’ message goes on to say they don’t regret any decision and would never have denied their daughter these life-saving treatments.

name: John Oliver
monologue: We still have no regrets. It’s blatant exploitation of my daughter’s medical situation.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, that mother felt that the story was blatant exploitation of her daughter’s medical situation — or, as I guess Bari would describe it, harnessing the punk energy of the new political realignment.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, I get her frustration at seeing misinformation about her daughter go far and wide. In fact, when we reached out to that mother, she told us, “I’ve been fighting for the truth about that damn Free Press article for a while.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And if you’re getting the sense that The Free Press isn’t about to let whatever fact-checking they do get in the way of a story they want to tell you, that also extends to some of the original reporting they do.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Take this piece they published last year about Austin, claiming crime had soared there under a progressive DA named José Garza. It prominently featured a billionaire named Daniel Lubetzky, the founder of Kind Snacks, who’d moved to Austin a few years earlier and was supporting a primary campaign to elect a more moderate DA.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The story claimed that Austin’s crime wave was leading many of its most buzzed-about new residents — and some of its wealthiest — to worry it might become the next San Francisco. But as local news there pointed out, there was a pretty big hole in that piece’s argument:

name: John Oliver
monologue: But this article from a website called The Free Press — one of the first lines (hopefully we can pop it up right here on the screen) — one of the first lines of the article claims crime in Austin has soared under a progressive district attorney. This morning, the numbers tell us that that is just not the case. We looked at crime reporting data from Austin police. So, in December of 2020, before José Garza took over, 20,500 crimes against people were committed throughout the entire year. A few years later, in 2023, with Garza as DA for a couple of years, the number was 2,000 fewer than in the same time frame.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, it’s true. And it is kind of striking that even local news was like, “Girl, calm down.” Because the only thing they usually love more than overhyping crime is, maybe, dogs running 5Ks. This just in: woof woof pant pant — good boy goes fast.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And finally, there’s this piece The Free Press recently posted about media coverage of young people starving in Gaza. It concerned photos that it said had helped convince a growing number of Americans that Israel has induced famine and is committing war crimes in Gaza.

name: John Oliver
monologue: There is a lot wrong with this article. For one thing, it questions how starvation and famine have been measured by claiming the IPC — the international body that helps monitor food insecurity and malnutrition — has quietly changed its methodology in Gaza, essentially redefining the criteria for determining a famine.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But that is false. Very basically, the IPC has multiple metrics for measuring malnutrition in children. One involves measuring height and weight; another involves arm circumference. Now, because arm circumference only requires a tape measure, it’s far easier to obtain, especially in a place like a war zone. So in Gaza, that is what they started using — because of, you know, all of this shit happening. And those methods were not, in fact, quietly introduced as The Free Press suggested, but have been accepted since 2019 and previously used in famine classifications in South Sudan and Sudan.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But it gets even grosser, because the piece tries to provide extra context for some pictures of starving children. And here’s one of its writers — the one who used to work for the Fuck-Hole Times — summing her work up:

name: John Oliver
monologue: So, you’ve probably seen these photos of skeletal kids in Gaza on front pages, all over social media, even in a UNICEF ad. They’ve become the symbols of famine. But we decided to look into these photos and the stories behind them. And what we found is that in case after case, these kids were sick — but not just with malnutrition. In every instance they were suffering with other conditions or illnesses, like cystic fibrosis, cerebral palsy, and even traumatic head injuries.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, their article claims all those kids were already facing grave situations because of their health irrespective of any third-party action. But a few things:

name: John Oliver
monologue: First, the traumatic head injury she mentioned was — as their article points out — caused by an Israeli shell explosion, which feels like a pretty significant third-party action.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Second, it’s not like the twelve photos they chose to look into are the only ones illustrating stories about famine in Gaza.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And as for the notion that this is something the mainstream media was ignoring, there is a key problem with that claim, too. See if you can spot it as she walks through their in-depth journalistic process:

name: John Oliver
monologue: We did something so simple, it’s shocking that no other journalist bothered to do it. So, this is how we figured this out. Let’s just take this example of Naja Hussein Haj, who appeared in CNN simply as suffering from severe malnutrition in Gaza City. So all we did is we took her name, we went to Google Translate, we took the Arabic spelling of her name, put that into Google, and pulled up a lot of local clips in which her parents were talking about what was really going on. And what we learned is that she has an esophagus condition — which is something that was even reported in English media, including The New York Times . That is a quite different and more nuanced story than the assumption that Israel wants her dead and they’re starving her.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, so if no other journalist bothered to do it, but it was even reported in The New York Times , that sure suggests the journalist very much did bother to do it.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But also, if we’re talking about context — when it comes to the child she mentioned there, they quote from an Arabic news outlet. Here is the whole section about her from that outlet. Here’s the translation, and here’s the quote The Free Press pulled, mentioning her ailments since birth, including vomiting while eating. But it’s worth noting the sentence before says, “Her condition worsens each day without access to protein- and vitamin-rich foods that are needed for her treatment.” And the line after reads, “During the Israeli war on the Gaza Strip, her condition deteriorated and she developed malnutrition because the right food for her was simply unavailable.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And while I would love to keep splitting hairs on whether a country’s starving kids is better or worse if those kids are already sick, let’s table that discussion for when I see you in hell!

name: John Oliver
monologue: That is not the only bit of cherry-picking in that piece, which features a lot of young people with, yes, pre-existing conditions or ailments that were made significantly worse when they couldn’t access food. And to be clear, as the president of Refugees International wrote, “People with underlying conditions always suffer first when hunger sets in,” adding that vulnerability is not a rebuttal of famine. It is a feature of how famine kills and who it hits first.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And it is kind of weird that nobody at The Free Press thought to include that sort of important context given that they are famously proud of their ability to Google shit!

name: John Oliver
monologue: And you should also know that piece circulated far and wide among those seeking to downplay the suffering in Gaza — including Bibi Netanyahu himself, who shared that video on his social media with the caption, “Facts matter.” Which is terrible for multiple reasons, including: if Netanyahu ever shared one of our stories, I think I’d burn this place to the fucking ground! And by the way, any story — even the one where I ate the ass of a cake bear that looks like me — if he retweeted that with a comment, “Facts matter,” you would never hear from us ever again!

name: John Oliver
monologue: Everything I’ve shown you so far should comfortably be enough to make you question the wisdom of putting Bari Weiss in charge of CBS News. But I still haven’t even gotten to her weirdest venture, which lays out her priorities and worldview pretty clearly: she has started her own university. Specifically, she’s co-founded the University of Austin (UATX) in Texas, and it is exactly what you’d expect. Here is one of the school’s promo videos:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] If you’re wondering why the museums you love and the publishing houses you love and the newspapers you used to trust — if you want to understand why they are hollowed out, you have to look at the nucleation point for this, and that is the university. The premise is that America is not only not great but evil to the core and rotten and needs to be torn down. The answer to that is simply no.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, there are so many things wrong with that — from the firm “no,” to the bullshit straw-man argument, to the claim we all have publishing houses we love that have been hollowed out, to the pretentiousness of the word nucleation point , which sounds like the title of a straight-to-streaming action flop starring Steven Seagal.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, UATX is currently unaccredited, and while Weiss proudly posted this image of students on the school’s first day, I should note that while that building does look impressive, that’s because it’s the Texas State Capitol. The actual school is housed on a couple of floors of a former department store in downtown Austin, which is pretty unusual. You don’t generally expect a college to suddenly pop up in an abandoned store like it’s a Spirit fucking Halloween!

name: John Oliver
monologue: While the school may not have a traditional campus, it does have a white-marble bust of Bari Weiss prominently displayed in one of its common areas. It was apparently donated by Joe Lonsdale, the billionaire co-founder of the defense contractor Palantir. He’s one of several billionaire donors to the school, along with Daniel Lubetzky (the Kind Snacks founder from that Austin crime-wave story) and Harlan Crow, famously Clarence Thomas’s benefactor.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So the school’s already got a lot of red flags even before you get to what’s being taught there. Its Substack — because of course it has one — brags that it’s a place where students quote Joseph Conrad and Joe Rogan in the same breath. And one of its big selling points is that its students adhere to what’s called the Chatham House rule, which essentially requires all classroom conversations be conducted off the record.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’ll let one of the school’s professors explain:

name: John Oliver
monologue: If someone says something unacceptable to people or shocking or problematic, you can’t run out and say, “Bobby said something racist,” or “Susie actually is a Zionist.” You cannot do this. And what that means is students don’t have to conform. They can actually say what they think.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Oh, that’s good. Well, in the spirit of saying what we think, I’ll go first: your vibe is all the way off. You look like Guillermo del Toro if he only directed episodes of Yellowstone . And you enunciate like you’re the third Crane brother that Frasier and Niles never talk about. And you can’t tell anyone I said that Chatham House rule!

name: John Oliver
monologue: If you’re wondering what sort of topics might require a rule like that, apparently one of their first offerings were summer classes called “The Forbidden Courses,” which promised to inquire honestly into today’s most vexing questions — illustrated with a photo of an instructor apparently pointing out hot-button statements for debate. If you zoom in, you’ll see it: “Non-Black people cannot use the n-word.” And suddenly that Chatham House rule makes a whole lot of sense, doesn’t it? Although any Black college student will tell you you don’t need to set up a whole university to find out which college kids are comfortable using the n-word — all it takes is a couple of rum-and-cokes and Lil Wayne on shuffle.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Look, it is no mystery what sort of person starts a university like this. But in case there were any doubt at all, just listen to Bari Weiss — not long after campus protests started over Gaza — spell out as clearly as possible what she wanted to see happen:

name: John Oliver
monologue: [Bari Weiss] Above all, starting today, we need to uproot, root and branch, the ideology that has supplanted truth at the core of American higher education. And that ideology goes by the name DEI. Some call it “wokeness,” or “anti-racism,” or “progressivism,” or “safety,” or “critical social justice,” or “identity Marxism.” Whatever term you use, what is clear is that this worldview has gained power in the world in a conceptual instrument called DEI.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. And that itself is a whole worldview right there. You know — this DEI thing that we’ve been trying, where we acknowledge not everyone’s been getting equal access to opportunity? Let’s just roll back the clock on that, shall we?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Also, let’s be anti-anti-racist and not think too much about what that might make us.

name: John Oliver
monologue: DEI is actually one of her favorite targets. She’s also said it’s undermining America , that it’s about arrogating power , and that it demonizes hard work, merit, family, and the dignity of the individual.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look — it is not new, or indeed interesting, that a commentator would say that. There are plenty of them out there, and there will always be an audience for those who want to make that case.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And the truth is, we wouldn’t even have done this story were it not for the fact that Bari Weiss has just been named editor-in-chief of CBS News. And that feels different.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Because there are many opinion-heavy outlets out there — from left to right, and with low to high editorial standards. This show is, among other things, an opinion outlet. And while our staff works incredibly hard to research stories before we write something, and vigorously check our facts afterward, we’re also not the news.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And I wouldn’t want anyone who led a pure opinion outlet — not even one that I happen to agree with — to suddenly be running CBS News. But it’s especially alarming to have someone doing it who has spent years putting out work that, in my opinion, is at best irresponsible and at worst deeply misleading.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, it’s not just about Bari Weiss being at CBS. It’s about the fact that CBS is now under the control of someone who thinks that she, and her editorial sensibility, make her a good fit for the job — and who, incidentally, is reportedly preparing a bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, home of CNN and, uh-oh, HBO. Which isn’t ideal.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Although, I’ve got to say — if what he likes about Bari is that she forces him to have hard conversations that get a bit uncomfortable — maybe he’ll like this.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But the thing is, it’s not just about Ellison either. Again, he’s just the latest in a string of billionaires who’ve taken over our journalistic institutions — from The Washington Post to The L.A. Times — and started making worrying changes.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And whatever complaints I might have had with their coverage before — and I have had plenty — my solution would never have been this.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Because when these takeovers get announced, it’s easy to think, “Well, thank goodness there are other outlets that aren’t under some billionaire’s influence.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That’s true — because there’s always another one. Until there suddenly isn’t.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And I admit, I don’t know what’s going to happen next. Maybe Bari Weiss will completely reshape CBS News. Maybe she’ll flame out and write another resignation letter heard around the world.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But it’s worth keeping an eye out for subtle changes there. Because while I’m sure many of CBS’s good journalists will continue to do great work, if you start seeing people resigning or getting fired — or you start seeing stories that seem off in some way, especially if they involve “the left going too far” on a topic Bari Weiss cares about — it’s worth asking yourself why that might be.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Because unfortunately, the much bigger answer might be that a billionaire has chosen to inject contrarian, right-leaning opinion journalism into an American icon — even if, much like that Thanksgiving Day Spider-Man, it has absolutely no fucking business being there.

name: Main Segment
monologue: Bari Weiss and CBS News Other segments:

name: My Point Is
monologue: the Upper West Side is more than just one thing!

name: John Oliver
monologue: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver Web exclusives Aired on October 19, 2025

name: John Oliver
monologue: John Oliver discusses the Air Bud franchise. Again. For even longer than he did last time. And for good reason, thank you very much!

name: John Oliver
monologue: Hello there, YouTube. We are off this week, but I’m here anyway with what we like to think of as exclusive bonus content—though, if you’re the kind of viewer who only watches our show on YouTube, you probably know it as worse content. I’m doing this because I wanted to talk about something important, namely, one of the wilder things to happen to the Air Bud franchise, which is already a pretty bold thing to say about a franchise that’s seen this happen.

name: John Oliver
monologue: T-minus three minutes to launch. 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, and blast off. “Even I’m lighter than a feather.” “How are we going to get home this time?” Space Buddies.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, Space Buddies is actually a canonical sequel to Air Bud , which probably comes as quite a shock to anyone only familiar with the original. It’d be like finding out they made a fourth sequel to Kramer vs. Kramer and it’s Kong: Skull Island. Wait, wait, hold on—did the boy in Kramer vs. Kramer grow up to be an adventurer? Is the boy Kong? I have so many questions.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, believe it or not, we actually talked about Air Bud three years ago, and you might have missed that. Or maybe you didn’t miss it—maybe you just saw a video titled Air Bud: Last Week Tonight , saw that it was almost 15 minutes long, and decided to do literally anything else with your time because you suddenly remembered how many lives you had.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, you don’t have to go and watch that segment to understand what I’m about to say. I would certainly recommend it, but you don’t have to do that. You also don’t need to watch the original movie Air Bud . I’ll give you a brief recap of both right now.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Very basically, Air Bud is about Josh, a kid whose dad eats it offscreen and who later finds a dog whom Josh steals from its original owner to recruit to his basketball team so they can win state—because there ain’t no rule against a dog playing basketball.

name: John Oliver
monologue: After that triumph, the dog’s original owner gets sent to jail for absolutely no reason, even though there are actually several rules against that happening. And that is essentially the plot of Air Bud , produced, by the way, by Harvey Weinstein. So, yeah, that’s fun.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, in our piece, I successfully argued that Air Bud ’s stated allegiance to rule-following was actually anything but that—that the movie’s relationship to rules was inconsistent and unpredictable, that 9/11 was a bummer, and that there’s too much kissing in movies. And I stand by every single point that I made in it.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And you might think that I shouldn’t have anything more to say about Air Bud , which is true—I shouldn’t. And yet, it turns out I very much do, because recently the masterminds behind the Air Bud franchise released a video that I personally take issue with.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Hey, I’m Robert Vince, the producer and creator of the 14-movie Air Bud franchise. We introduced the world to an incredible golden retriever called Air Bud. He proved to the world that anything is possible.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, stop right there. Now, I should say right away that isn’t the part that I take issue with. Although, I do want to point out that it makes a lot of sense that this guy thought a dog who could bounce a basketball was impressive enough to build a movie empire around, given that he handles the ball like he’s afraid he’ll break it.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Also, I want to say three small things before moving on to the big thing.

name: John Oliver
monologue: First, 14 is just too many movies. It seems cosmically unjust to me that there are 14 Air Bud movies and still just three Bill & Ted s, two Freaky Fridays , and one lonely Michael Clayton. Yeah, I’m just saying—they put buddies on the moon. Don’t tell me they can’t make a Michael Clayton Goes to France , Michael Clayton: The Colleges , or Michael Clayton Scared Stupids. They could, and they should.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Second, far be it from me to explain the Air Bud franchise to the guy who created it, but the golden retriever in question was not actually called Air Bud. The movie is called that. The dog is called Buddy—or alternately Blue by his original owner, an alcoholic clown currently serving a prison sentence for reasons never once explained.

name: John Oliver
monologue: In fact, according to The Dog Could Definitely Ball: An Oral History of Air Bud , the movie’s director never even liked that title, believing it sounded less elegant than the movie he was trying to make, adding, “I was saying we should call the movie Buddy because that was the dog’s name. But there had just been a movie called Buddy with a chimpanzee or something.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, we could debate the elegance of the title—or indeed the movie. We could even debate whether they should have gone with a much clearer title like, not for nothing, The Dog Could Definitely Ball. But what we can’t debate—what I won’t debate—is that Robert Vince introduced America to a dog named Air Bud. Because he did not do that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: It would have been weird for Josh to name the random dog he’s using to replace his father Air Bud. It’s maybe the second weirdest name he could have gone with, right after “Better Dad.

name: John Oliver
monologue: The point is, Vince didn’t introduce America to a dog named Air Bud any more than Spielberg introduced America to a shark named Jaws , or Pete Docter introduced America to a house named Up , or James Cameron introduced America to a blue alien named Avatar. Because for the record, the names of the characters they introduced America to are respectively Buddy, Bruce the Shark, Houses Don’t Have Names, and—truly—who can say.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And finally, as for Vince’s claim that Buddy the dog “proved to the world that anything was possible.” Did he? Did he do that? Because I’d argue that the original Air Bud proved that one very good dog could, despite some obvious defensive weaknesses, play some rudimentary basketball.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Though I am duty bound to remind you, he did only score four field goals in his one game. Honestly, the main thing that’s impressive isn’t that they trained a dog to bite a ball into a basket—it’s that someone managed to milk that single dumb trick into, again, a 14-film franchise.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Anyway, these are my thoughts so far on the—and this is true—first 11 seconds of that video. Luckily, we’re about to get to the point.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, we’re bringing Buddy back to the big screen with an all-new movie called Air Bud Returns.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, now that is right. Air Bud Returns is going to be the 15th movie in the Air Bud franchise, and apparently it’s going to be a more grounded return to its basketball roots while crucially deviating from the original’s formula in a pretty meaningful way.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Because, according to the actual press release, Air Bud Returns centers on a 12-year-old boy who’s always dreamt of being a star basketball player—check—and after the passing of his father (his dad eats it too—double check), he finds, you’ll never guess, a stray golden retriever he names Buddy.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But wait, because I’m not done. He also apparently discovers an original VHS of the Air Bud movie in his dead-as-hell father’s belongings, which—I’m sorry, what? What?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Look, I can get behind the Air Bud franchise reaching the heights of space. I can even get behind the basketball dog saving Christmas—twice, by the way. But what I cannot do is wrap my brain around an Air Bud that takes place in a universe that also has Air Bud the movie, which is to say nothing of the reality-straining suggestion that someone would hang onto a VHS tape until 2025.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’m supposed to believe that the kid’s dad dies and he comes across both a basketball dog and a movie about a kid with a dead dad who befriends a basketball dog—and that kid doesn’t then freak the fuck out? No, instead he says, “Oh, maybe I’ll play basketball like the kid in this movie whose life weirdly matches my own almost perfectly.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And the craziest thing of all is we are still not at the main thing that I have an issue with here. So, let’s once again pick up that announcement where we left off.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Today, we have big news. For the first time ever, we’re opening up the auditions for the next Air Bud.” “No way.” “Let me introduce you to lead animal trainer Mark Forbes.” “We’re launching a nationwide search for our final star. We need a dog who is a purebred golden retriever, who’s athletic, and ideally he would love basketball—just like the original Air Bud.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’m sorry—you don’t have the dog yet? You are trying to crowdsource the dog? In the words of Josh’s dad from the original Air Bud , I think I’m in hell, because this is completely insane.

name: John Oliver
monologue: In fact, it is so insane I don’t even have time to register the weirdness of announcing your dog search while the most Air Bud -looking dog I’ve ever seen is sitting right next to you. It’s like a casting director making a video asking for a Timothy Chalamet type while standing next to a well-trained but heartbroken Finn Wolfhard. It is a fucking insult.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But regardless, announcing you’re making another Air Bud movie when you don’t have a dog on standby that can play basketball is audacious. It’s akin to proudly announcing you’re making a season of White Lotus without a beautiful location secured, or a Fast and Furious movie without access to any cars, or a Tom Hardy movie without a weird little voice for him to do. Those are the key things everyone’s expecting from you.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So Air Bud Returns isn’t anything without a dog who can play basketball. Without that, your idea is basically just movie.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And what’s worse is Robert Vince even then has the gall to try and turn this deficiency into an inspirational speech at the end of the video.

name: John Oliver
monologue: This is your chance to be part of the Air Bud legacy. Ain’t no rule said the dog can’t play basketball. When you get the chance, you’re always taking a shot.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Listen. Listen. You can dress it up with soaring music and misleading cutaways suggesting you can play basketball when you can’t. After all, that is most—if crucially not all—of the formula for Air Bud. But at a certain point, you really do need a dog who can shoot a basketball.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And look, there is no shame in not having one. Most people don’t. I’d argue it’s the single largest roadblock keeping people from making dog-playing-basketball movies. The reason no one made Air Bud movies before the movie Air Bud was because no one had an Air Bud until somebody did. And that is when they made an Air Bud movie.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And it’s not like you can just make another Buddy the dog out of thin air. Although honestly, if you cared enough, you actually could. The dog’s original owner apparently froze 11 vials of the original Buddy’s semen, meaning—and I quote—“There are still a couple vials of Air Bud cum left stored in a freezer at the International Canine Semen Bank,” which is just an all-time sentence in the English language. I’m not even going to stop down to discuss that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Apparently, we went from 11 vials to a couple, even though I have a number of questions about that. Because look, as galling as it is that they are crowdsourcing the single most important part of their basketball dog movie, I will say not everyone seemed to have an issue with it.

name: John Oliver

name: John Oliver

More, I’m sure, but reportedly five.

name: John Oliver
monologue: John Oliver details what Medicare Advantage is, why it basically has all the pitfalls of private insurance, and the economic significance of novelty slippers. You’ll see.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Our main story tonight concerns healthcare. Ostensibly the subject matter of the pit, which is slightly about healthcare, but much more about the gentle head tilt of Noah Wy on behalf of several members of my staff. Engulf me in that hoodie, you casual Friday hero. Specifically, we’re going to talk about Medicare, the federal program for those 65 or older or with qualifying disabilities. Now, open enrollment for it began on October 15th and will run through December 7th. And it’s why this time of year sees tons of ads like these.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Hi, I’m Joe Nameoth. If you’re on Medicare, this is important information.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Hi, William Shatner here with a new message about Medicare benefits.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Hi, I’m Jimmy JJ Walker. If you’re on Medicare, listen to this.

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’m Meredith Vieira. What’s complicated and confusing that many people over 65 deal with each year? Medicare.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Okay, this isn’t the point, but the question, what’s complicated and confusing that people over 65 deal with each year is just too broad given that the answer is everything. Everything confuses them. Have you ever seen a 70-year-old try to work an Apple TV remote? It’s actually the reason Biden dropped out of the race last year. Apparently, his team handed him an Amazon Fire Stick right before that debate, and we all know what happened next.

name: John Oliver
monologue: These ads are ubiquitous. One analysis found that in Medicare’s open enrollment period a few years ago, over half a million ads like those aired on TV, that’s over 8,000 a day. Normally, for an ad to be that overplayed, it needs to feature a child’s band singing a song that makes you want to commit mass murder. But while they’re often framed as being about Medicare, they’re actually promoting something called Medicare Advantage.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And that is different because while Medicare Advantage has the word Medicare in it, it is not what you may think. It’s not health insurance provided directly to you by the government. Instead, it’s a different system where the government pays private insurers, typically owned by companies like these to administer your benefits for you. Honestly, it probably shouldn’t have the word Medicare anywhere near it because it’s misleading. It’s kind of like the mountain chicken. Picture what a mountain chicken looks like in your head right now. Do you have it? You’re wrong cuz it’s this. It’s a frog, which is just wrong. Mountain chicken sounds like at minimum a chicken that lives in the mountains or what a starving stranded hiker would call human flesh. It’s just mountain chicken. It’s mountain chicken. It’s definitely not Jeff. What it does not sound like though is this. That is a misuse of words.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Anyway, the point is, thanks to blanket advertising and the fact some employee retirement packages offer these plans exclusively, more than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries are now enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan, and a percentage expected to grow to nearly two-thirds by 2034, which is concerning because these plans can have real issues. One expert has said the best candidate for Medicare Advantage is someone who’s healthy. We see trouble when someone gets sick. But that is a problem because statistically most people will get sick. It’s just a fact of life. Like all hamsters die, most cats hate you. And if Jeremy Allen White is on screen, he is sweating. Acting is sweating. We all know that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And that’s by no means the only flaw here. Because as you will see, while these plans can be great for companies’ bottom lines, they can be woefully insufficient for those who signed up for them and the providers who have to deal with them. Medicare Advantage basically has all the problems of private insurance but applies to a more vulnerable population.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So given that tonight, let’s talk about Medicare Advantage — what it is, what the coverage can be like, and whether you or someone you know should sign up. But to understand it, you first need to understand how Medicare works, which already isn’t easy because, as you’ll know if you’ve ever enrolled in it yourself or had to help someone else do it, it is confusing. On a scale of one to Inception , it is basically Tenet . And I don’t say that lightly.

name: John Oliver
monologue: To put it very simply, Medicare currently has four components: Part A, B, C, and D. Part A covers hospital and other inpatient care. That’s what you’ve paid into your whole life. And for most, you can enroll at 65 with no additional premium due. Part B covers doctor’s visits and outpatient services. Now, you do have to pay a monthly premium for that. That’s typically taken out of your social security check. And even then, it only covers 80% of your cost — the remaining 20% you have to pay for out of pocket. But you can buy a separate Medigap plan to cover that, which typically costs $200 or more a month.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And that gap is something ads pushing Medicare Advantage like to highlight — like this one featuring Kelsey Grammar.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Stop it. You stop it right now, Frasier. Though, to be fair, that is not the creepiest thing he’s ever said about the medical profession, given his memoir features the quote, “Nice girls made me really nervous, claustrophobic.” But broken women, women in pain, women looking to be fixed, are for these women the doctor was in. That is on the back cover. And it is wild to publish a book where you essentially argue if you **** me, you might need professional help.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Anyway, that is part B. Now, if you want prescription drugs — and if you’re a senior citizen, you definitely do — you need to pay for a separate Part D premium which helps cover those. And that leaves us with Part C, which is Medicare Advantage. It functions as an alternative to all the other parts in that it helps cover hospitals, doctor visits, and usually drugs, while offering often extra benefits like some dental, vision, and hearing coverage or even debit cards to help pay grocery bills. And it does all of that for a relatively low upfront cost, as other than that standard premium taken out of your social security check, over three-quarters of enrollees pay no additional premium at all. So, it is pretty appealing on the surface.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And while I don’t have to show you one more ad for it, especially as it basically recaps everything I just said, I’m going to do it anyway because it is magnificent.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Honey, we already have Medicare. Why do I need to call?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Alan, the Feldman said we may be able to get additional benefits with a Medicare Advantage plan right here in our zip code with zero monthly premiums.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Honey, what do you mean additional benefits? We turned 65, we got Medicare. That’s all there is to it, right?

name: John Oliver
monologue: I’m talking about Medicare Part C, commonly called Medicare Advantage. We have traditional Medicare, which is only Medicare Parts A and B, but not Part C.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Wait, so not everyone on Medicare is a Part C plan?

name: John Oliver
monologue: No. That’s why we need to call because there may be plans available with additional benefits that aren’t covered under Medicare Parts A and B. We don’t have a Medicare Part C plan, which covers everything in Part A and Part B, plus extra benefits in Medicare Part C.

name: John Oliver
monologue: There are great plans that may be available with extra benefits like dental, vision, and hearing.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That is, and this is true, only the first half of that commercial. It has it all — amateur porn-level acting, wild physical gestures, the totally unnecessary undercurrent of a broken marriage, and the phrase “right here in our zip code.” It is perfect. I also love the disclaimer saying “paid actor portrayal,” as if we’ve been so sucked in by the natural delivery of concussed Rob Reiner and overcaffeinated Amy Sedaris here that we might need to be reminded.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But the thing is, there are a lot of drawbacks to Medicare Advantage plans. For a start, they come at an inflated cost to taxpayers, which is a bit weird given that a big part of the argument for creating this system over two decades ago was that bringing in private insurers would help control costs. In fact, here is Orrin Hatch back then, one of its biggest cheerleaders, making his pitch.

name: John Oliver
monologue: ORRIN HATCH (archival): Choice, the right to pick the coverage you want. That’s what Medicare Advantage actually gives you. Now, there are those who believe that socialism is the answer to everything. Let government do it. Government can do it more efficiently. Well, if you believe that, you haven’t watched the last 50 years.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. The whole argument was that it would expand choice and companies would do a better job at controlling costs than the government. And look, some things are better when the private sector’s involved. Take novelty slippers. Only through competition in the free market do you get innovations like hairy feet slippers, creepy Marge Simpson slippers, Sigmund Freud slippers, Danny DeVito slippers, and golden penis slippers. And if you’re wondering who would buy those, you are looking at him right here.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, why did I buy these? I don’t know. Probably because of something deep-rooted in my psyche stemming from my childhood. At least according to my Sigmund Freud slipper right here.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But sadly, sadly, the private sector hasn’t done as well with Medicare as it has with slippers, because these plans have never saved the government money. In fact, a report last year estimated Medicare Advantage had cost the government, over the previous 18 years, an extra $591 billion . And this is partly down to the fact that the major companies involved need to make profits for their investors. And they have found ways to do that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: One concerns how they get paid. Because in traditional Medicare, a provider treats you and the government pays a fee for it. But in Medicare Advantage, plans get a fixed payment from the government for each member they take on, regardless of whether you get treatment or not. And crucially, that payment’s based in large part on what illnesses you’re listed as having, because insurers are entitled to extra money when their patients are diagnosed with conditions that are costly to treat. Here’s a report from several years ago explaining how it basically works.

name: John Oliver
monologue: REPORTER (archival): The insurance company uses what are known as diagnosis codes to report that person’s level of sickness to the government.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Well, they pay one rate for plain old diabetes and then they pay another rate for diabetes with complications. If you write down in the file that the patient has diabetes and has complications with eyesight or other things, they’ll get paid a higher rate.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Right? And in theory, that makes sense. You want insurers to take care of sicker patients. Unfortunately, a lot of things that sound good turn out to be terrible in practice — like overalls on adults, or drinking a beer, or buying a flight that leaves at 6:00 a.m. to save money. Oh, sure, seems like a good idea until you’re at the airport at 4 in the morning. But hey, at least you got to your destination by 10:00 a.m. and can’t check into your hotel for another five hours. Aren’t you glad you saved $35 on that ticket?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Well, the same is true here, because the government paying more for sicker patients has given insurers an incentive to identify as many health conditions as possible for each enrollee — and potentially to then game the system. They can find lots of ways to add big-money diagnoses to patients’ charts through a practice known as upcoding .

name: John Oliver
monologue: This happens a lot. One investigation found that Medicare paid insurers about $50 billion over three years for diagnoses added just by insurers. Not only that, many diagnoses were added for which patients then received no treatment. And often neither the patients nor their doctors had any idea — which isn’t great, is it? The whole point of a doctor is for them to diagnose you. Or in my case, for them to look down at the chart, look at me again, back at the chart, and then say, “48 years old? Are we sure about that?

name: John Oliver
monologue: And while insurers will claim they’re just being thorough, they’ve been repeatedly accused of essentially pulling a Munchausen by paperwork . In 2022, The Times found eight of the ten biggest Medicare Advantage insurers had submitted inflated bills according to federal audits, and that four of the five largest players had faced federal lawsuits alleging that efforts to over-diagnose their customers had crossed the line into fraud.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And some have been accused of getting very sneaky to add patient codes. For instance, many tout home visits with ads featuring happy seniors excitedly greeting healthcare workers at their door. Here is how UnitedHealthcare advertises theirs.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. And you can see how attractive that is. Not least because the senior gets a visitor, and you know how happy that makes them. The elderly love exactly three things: having guests, talking to guests, and then freaking out when that guest sits in their chair.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But an investigation found that in programs like that one, companies push nurses to run screening tests and add unusual diagnoses, turning the roughly hour-long stops in patients’ homes into an extra $1,800 per visit on average. And while UnitedHealthcare will insist most of the conditions it’s coded for in its House Calls program haven’t raised payment, some very much have.

name: John Oliver
monologue: For instance, documents show its software would suggest the diagnosis of secondary hyperaldosteronism, a condition in which levels of the hormone aldosterone rise — without requiring it be confirmed by a lab test. UnitedHealthcare apparently diagnosed that nearly a quarter million times after home visits, leading to $450 million in government payments over just three years. Even though a former House Calls nurse said, “In a million years, I wouldn’t have come up with a diagnosis of secondary hyperaldosteronism.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But of course not. I didn’t even know what hyperaldosteronism was before working on this piece. And to be honest, I still don’t really know much about it — aside from the fact that you can rearrange the letters to spell “modernist horseplay,” which isn’t nothing, but it does feel close to it.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, I have to tell you, UnitedHealthcare claims that report misrepresents House Calls, which is just about supplementing doctor’s visits and identifying gaps in patient care. I presume that they’re currently making that same argument to the DOJ’s criminal healthcare fraud unit, which is investigating its Medicare billing practices. And I wish them the very best of luck with that.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But they are not the only company who faced these sorts of accusations. An insurer called Independent Health faced similar claims, including that a woman in one of their Advantage plans was apparently coded for prostate cancer because, according to an internal email, “when a married couple has any disease, both were assigned to that disease,” which is both ridiculous and also kind of romantic.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Do you, Tracy, promise to take Doug’s diseases from tip to taint as long as you both shall live? I do. I really do.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now again, I have to tell you, Independent Health did not admit liability, but they did pay $98 million to settle that lawsuit. You know, the exact kind of thing you do when you’re not liable for something.

name: John Oliver
monologue: So, at this point, I think it’s pretty clear these plans aren’t a particularly good use of taxpayer money. But are they good for patients? Well, on the surface, cheaper premiums sound appealing. And if you’re relatively healthy, these plans can seem like the more attractive option. Just listen to this woman explaining why she and her husband picked one.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Right. And I get that that makes sense for her right now, because from the minute I saw that woman, I knew she played pickleball. She didn’t need to tell me that. Everything about her screams, “I’ll dink your kitchen then cross-court lob until we bagel, because guess what — we la the pickle, bitch.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And Medicare Advantage plans go out of their way to recruit people like her. Many even offer perks like gym memberships, which can be disproportionately attractive to relatively healthy beneficiaries.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But once you get sick, you can find out your plan has a lot of limitations. For example, under regular Medicare, you can go to any doctor or hospital that takes it — which is most of them. But with Medicare Advantage, as with most private insurance, you can typically only use doctors in the plan’s network and service area. And as those can change at any time, a doctor who is in-network when you sign up can quickly fall out of it — and that can be a big problem.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Consider this woman who had cancer, who qualified for Medicare due to disability, but signed up for a Medicare Advantage plan thinking that it would save her money.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That is absurd. Her doctor was in network, but the building wasn’t. It’s one of those things that makes your brain hurt if you think about it for too long — like how gravity works, or why some people’s bodies fart when they’re scared, or how Bill Bixby’s daughter was 17 years old the year his girlfriend was born. Some things are just too difficult for you to comprehend.

name: John Oliver
monologue: But it can be genuinely hard to find someone in network on an Advantage plan. And even if its list of providers looks good on paper, it can quickly collapse under the slightest inspection, as this man discovered:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah, of course it isn’t. And finding out half your list is just grocery store pharmacies would be frustrating, because everybody knows you don’t go there for an endocrinology appointment. You go there to check your blood pressure in the machine that makes your arm feel like it’s being squeezed by Paul Mescal’s thighs. That is a thing that we all do.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And that is not a one-off either. One review found the majority of Medicare Advantage organizations had between 30 to 60% inaccurate locations in their directories. But even if you can find a provider, you may then have to deal with something called prior authorizations.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Now, you’re probably familiar with them from employer-sponsored plans. While traditional Medicare almost always pays for the care your doctor says you qualify for, virtually all enrollees in Medicare Advantage are required to obtain prior authorization for some services. While these plans are supposed to cover all medically necessary services that original Medicare does, actually getting approval can be a grueling process. As this doctor explains:

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. And everything about that sounds like a nightmare — including the presence of the words “fax machine.” I thought we’d stopped making them around the same time we stopped making good romantic comedies. In fact, I think the last time I saw a fax machine, a frazzled Michelle Pfeiffer was getting horned up for George Clooney. Remember that? Remember good romantic comedies? The kind of films that feel like a blanket and make you leak from all your holes. What happened to this country?

name: John Oliver
monologue: Anyway, as you might guess, Medicare Advantage providers partly or fully deny millions of prior authorizations each year , and that can be maddening for those who need care. Take what happened to Gary Bent. He had significant complications from brain surgery, including being unable to stand or walk on his own. His doctors said he needed a lengthy stay at a highly skilled rehab center. Now, under traditional Medicare, that would have been covered. But he had a Medicare Advantage plan from UnitedHealthcare, which only approved him for a few weeks at a short-term rehab facility.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And Gary’s wife and daughter remember the advice that they got from his care team about trying to appeal United’s decisions.

name: John Oliver
monologue: GARY’S WIFE: They told me I would probably win one or two, maybe even three. But then the speed with which these denials came would increase. They would be fewer and fewer days apart, and eventually I was going to lose.

name: John Oliver
monologue: GARY’S DAUGHTER: We felt like this process was designed to wear us out. And I would say it did wear us out.

name: John Oliver
monologue: Yeah. And that’s exactly what happened. They won two appeals, then lost a third after an external reviewer sided with the company. While UnitedHealthcare insists it was just following Medicare guidelines, Gary was sent home before his family felt he was ready — with, by the way, a fever and neck pain. And within 11 hours of being discharged, he was rushed to the ER, where he was diagnosed with meningitis. And that was just one step in a quick decline toward him dying the following winter — a decline that his wife says was made worse by the added trauma of having to fight for the care he needed and was entitled to.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And there are some things so awful it’s almost impressive to be able to make them worse. It’s like seeing a Cybertruck with Diddy’s face painted on it. I don’t know how you managed to do it, but I like this even less.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And the thing is, delaying, underpaying, or denying care doesn’t just hurt patients — it hurts hospitals, too, particularly those in rural areas, because they don’t have the time or resources to sink into constantly appealing decisions, which has had real consequences.

name: John Oliver
monologue: REPORTER (archival): This was once the geriatric psychiatry unit at Alliance Healthcare in Holly Springs, Mississippi. Now, the hallways hollow and beds sitting empty. This operating room only a few years ago was doing five or six procedures a day. Now zero. Dr. Kenneth Williams is the CEO. He says the hospital can no longer afford the unit or any inpatient care for that matter.

name: John Oliver
monologue: That is terrible. Thanks to Medicare Advantage, that whole wing is now abandoned — and by the looks of it, already haunted, because at any moment it feels like Jigsaw is about to pop out with a realtor to just check out the space.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And even hospitals which haven’t had to close wings have stopped taking these plans, with a 2023 survey finding nearly 20% of health systems had stopped accepting at least one Medicare Advantage plan that year alone.

name: John Oliver
monologue: And if you’re thinking, “Well, you know what, that’s okay. If I get sick and I need a specialist, I’ll just switch back to regular Medicare,” — you may not be able to, because remember, it has that 20% gap that you need to cover. Now, when you first enroll, it’s easy to buy a Medigap plan to do that, because they can’t hold preexisting conditions against you.
